models.title: AI-enabled gravitational-waves searches for binary neutron stars at optimal sensitivity
models.authors: Bhavya Gupta, Deep Chatterjee, William Benoit, Ethan Marx, Christina Reissel, Seiya Tsukamoto, Kyungseop Yoon, Michael W. Coughlin, Philip Harris, Erik Katsavounidis
models.venue: arXiv preprint (LIGO DCC P2600320; no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF text read in full; Fig 4 read visually; Figs 5b, 6, 7, 9 not viewed).
models.architecture: Aframe-BNS: Aframe's modified 1D ResNet-34 (group norm in place of batch norm, 1D convolutions, single sigmoid output) with a new heterodyne pre-processing front end. Whitened H1 and L1 strain is heterodyned (de-chirped, phase-only 0PN term, eq. 3) against N reference chirp masses, the average-pooled heterodyned series of the two detectors are added in quadrature (eq. 4), the top k=10 chirp-mass channels by peak value are kept, and the last 1.5 s of each is stacked into 2k=20 input channels (H1,L1 for each of 10 channels). Same ResNet-34 otherwise as the BBH search (marx2024).
models.inputs: 2048 Hz H1,L1 strain; each training element is a 30 s segment: first 20 s give a per-channel PSD that whitens the remaining 10 s, 1 s trimmed each edge leaving 8 s; injections are added before whitening; 8 s windows are heterodyned and the final 1.5 s fed to the network. PSD from 64 s of preceding data at inference (8 s in training).
models.data: O3 public GWOSC strain, analysis-ready H1/L1 coincident segments. Training background 2019-11-01 to 2020-01-05 (O3b; 15,000 s held for validation); test stretch 2019-05-09 to 2019-06-08 (O3a). Time-slides generate signal-free background (training: random independent H1/L1 draws separated by more than the light travel time; inference: 10 years of live-time by shifting L1). 30,000 BNS waveforms (IMRPhenomPv2, 25 s, m1 triangular up to 2.5 Msun, m2 in (1,m1), spin<0.4, z<0.15; 10,000 for training and 20,000 for validation as stated); ~4e5 test signals sampled of which ~8e4 injected after rejecting network SNR<4.
models.training: Binary cross-entropy; dynamic on-the-fly injection with SNR rescaling; curriculum (first 3 epochs network SNR drawn from a power law between 30 and 100, then 8-100); augmentations: time reversal, amplitude inversion, H1/L1 swap and one-detector muting of the signal (tagged negative). Batch 2000, 200 batches per epoch, ~2e5 steps (~1016 epochs, ~4e8 examples), ~96 h on one NVIDIA H200. Validation metric AUROC up to FPR 1e-3.
models.results: Sensitive volume vs FAR for BNS populations (log-normal around 1.4, 1.6, 1.8, 2.0 Msun, width 0.1) compared with GWTC-3 matched-filter numbers: Aframe-BNS is ~10% below MBTA/PyCBC-Hyperbank for 1.4+1.4 (about level with GstLAL at the lowest FAR), matches them at 1.6+1.6, and exceeds them for 1.8+1.8 (+10 to +15%) and 2.0+2.0 (+25 to +40%). On the O3 mock data challenge (1790 injections, 1<m<2.05 Msun, SNR>8) at FAR<1/month Aframe recovers 671 vs MBTA 648, GstLAL 528, SPIIR 462, PyCBC 286; at 1/year 572 vs 619/497/414/187. In Gaussian aLIGO ZDHP noise Aframe-BNS reaches a ~160 Mpc sensitive distance at 1/month (Schafer et al. 2023: ~50 Mpc); in real O3 noise ~120 Mpc. Online: 172 us per sample, 22 ms per batch of 128, 4.7 s median end-to-end latency, 450 s of two-detector data per second per GPU in offline mode.
models.code: No code statement in the paper. The Aframe code base (github.com/ML4GW/aframe, MIT, pushed 2026-10) contains heterodyne and BNS configs (projects/train/configs/time_heterodyne.yaml, bns.yaml, projects/export/export_heterodyne.yaml); no trained weights in the repo tree.

models.title: Detection and Mitigation of Glitches in LISA Data: A Machine Learning Approach
models.authors: Niklas Houba, Luigi Ferraioli, Domenico Giardini
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF text read in full except appendix spectrograms; confusion matrices recomputed from the extracted figure counts).
models.architecture: Three-network pipeline on LISA TDI 2.0 data. (1) CNN anomaly detector (TensorFlow): two 3x3 conv layers with 32 filters, four with 64, ReLU, 2x2 max-pool after each pair, flatten, dense 64-64-32, one output (same net regresses the anomaly injection time; negative output = no anomaly). Input: 32x256 two-channel image of E_Y(t) and E_Z(t) TDI combinations. (2) Hybrid 'wide and deep' NN: wide branch (64,32, ReLU, L2, batch-norm) plus deep branch (64,64,32), softmax over 25 classes; input is a 24x3 table of glitch-to-noise ratios (GNR) from template matching of the CNN-estimated FRED glitch against the TDI response of all 24 possible injection points (18 interferometer points + 6 test-mass points) and a GW-burst class. (3) Stacked LSTM (six layers of 50 units, tanh, dense 1-unit output) acting as a TDI inverter that estimates the glitch time series from the two affected TDI channels; FRED rise/fall times first optimised by differential evolution (SciPy).
models.inputs: TDI 2.0 Michelson variables at 4 Hz in frequency units from the LISA consortium simulators (lisaglitch, lisainstrument, lisagwresponse, pyTDI; FREDS2 stochastic glitch model, SciRDv1 noise, static unequal arm lengths). CNN: 7.5 min segments (1792 samples), moving average (20), absolute value, normalisation to [0,1], 16x1792 image per channel, resized to 256 wide, two combinations stacked to 32x256.
models.data: Simulated only. Glitch durations seconds-15 min, strength 5-200% of max quasi-stationary noise amplitude, rise time 1-200 s; also GW bursts. CNN: 250,000 training / 20,000 test samples (both stages; second stage anomaly-only). WDNN: 150,000 train / 20,000 test. LSTM: 100,000 samples per glitch case. No real or LISA Pathfinder data.
models.training: CNN: Adam lr 5e-4, MSE loss, 50 epochs, batch 16, best weights on an independent validation set (two stages, classification then injection-time). LSTM: Adam lr 1e-3, MSE, retrained for each injection point and FRED parameter set (a 'low-latency' variant is trained on a range of FRED parameters, with lower accuracy). WDNN training details not given beyond sample counts.
models.results: CNN detection: 100% of non-anomalous test segments correctly labelled, 99.99915% of anomalous detected; injection time error mean zero, std 3.995 s (fast-rising <20 s: <1 s error, slow-rising worse). WDNN: GW bursts recognised in 98.187% of cases, 0.065% of FREDS2 glitches called bursts, glitch injection point correct 92.085% of the time (vs 68.613% for highest-GNR selection alone); misclassification mostly between inter-spacecraft interferometer ij and reference interferometer ji. With injection-time std reduced to 3.0 s overall accuracy rises to ~94.6% (recomputed). After LSTM subtraction 93.93% of calibrated TDI segments are classified anomaly-free by the CNN.
models.code: No code link or data statement in the paper. Relies on public LISA simulators (lisaglitch etc.). GitHub searches found no repository for this pipeline.
models.gaps: Simulated glitches from the authors' own FRED/FREDS2 family; no LISA Pathfinder data. No false-alarm rate or ROC for the CNN detector (only TN/TP fractions on a mixed test set; class balance of the 20,000 test samples not given); Fig 11 ROC/AUC values not extracted. LSTM mitigation quantified only by the CNN re-detection rate and a few examples (three glitch cases tested in full, no residual-noise requirement comparison). No effect on parameter estimation shown despite the abstract's claim of reduced biases.

models.title: Detection and Prediction of Future Massive Black Hole Mergers with Machine Learning and Truncated Waveforms
models.authors: Niklas Houba, Stefan H. Strub, Luigi Ferraioli, Domenico Giardini
models.venue: arXiv preprint (no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF text read in full except the appendix spectrograms; Fig 8 and Fig 14 read visually).
models.architecture: Two-stage LISA early-warning prototype. (1) Detection CNN (the glitch-detector architecture of houba2024glitch re-used): two 3x3 conv layers with 32 filters, four with 64, ReLU, 2x2 max-pool after each pair, dense 64-64-32, one output; it regresses the vertical pixel position of the inspiral trace in a time-evolving TDI 2.0 A-channel spectrogram and a positive output is a detection. (2) Time-to-merger prediction by deep reinforcement learning: a deep-Q/actor-critic agent with continuous actions (maximum horizon 100 h, 20 h for the 'region-specific' agent), rewards generated from truncated-waveform template matching (reward filtering, adaptive learning rate and supervised policy fine-tuning against noisy rewards, two training stages).
models.inputs: Detection: black and white spectrograms of TDI 2.0 A built from the most recent 10 days of 4 Hz data, updated as new data arrive (reduced resolution). RL state: history buffer of 83 h of TDI data, cadence 60 s (template matching 5 s in simulation, 50 min in the Spritz example).
models.data: Simulated. Detection training: 250,000 merger events (component masses 1e5-1e7 Msun, luminosity distance up to 100 Gpc as in LISA Spritz), 100 random 10-day windows each from one month before merger to minutes before (2.5 M spectrograms) plus 2.5 M merger-free spectrograms; noise per the LISA science requirements. Test: 20,000 events with the Table I parameters (m1 = 3e5, 3e6, 3e7 Msun, q=1/3, spins 0.5/0.7, 15 Gpc), 20,000 at 15-20 Gpc, 20,000 merger-free. RL: IMRPhenomD signals, masses 1e6-1e7 Msun, distances to 100 Gpc, mergers separated by 20-100 h; 25,000 events for ideal-reward pre-training, 25,000 for noisy-reward fine-tuning, 5,000 test events. Validation on the LISA Spritz challenge MBH merger (m1 = 1.32e6 Msun, q=0.463, SNR ~2000, glitches and gaps removed).
models.training: CNN trained on the labelled spectrograms (optimiser details not given beyond the cited glitch paper). RL: discount 0.93, epsilon 1 decaying at 0.9998 per step, history 83 h, learning rates 5e-7, Rmax 90, reward sensitivity 0.005, target update tau 0.005 (multi-agent hyper-parameter search, Table II); two stages (ideal rewards, then noisy template-matching rewards with supervised actor fine-tuning re-applied every 50 mergers).
models.results: Detection (Fig 8): at 15 Gpc the CNN detects (read from figure) >=95% of m1=3e5 events already 1 month pre-merger, ~34% of 3e6 events and ~5% of 3e7 events, rising to >=98% for all masses by 5 h before merger; detection is harder for heavier systems; 20 Gpc is a few points lower. Time-to-merger prediction (Fig 14): mean absolute error of the global RL agent is below truncated template matching until ~16-20 h before merger (about 12.5 h vs ~23 h at 30 h pre-merger) and above it afterwards (4.2 h vs 3 h at 10 h; 2.3 h vs ~1 h at merger); a region-specific agent trained for the last 20 h reaches ~3.6 h at 20 h and ~1.0 h at 0 h, beating template matching. On the Spritz event the CNN detects the signal ~20 days before the merger.
models.code: No code or data statement in the paper. Relies on public LISA simulators and the Spritz data challenge. GitHub searches found no repository.
models.gaps: No false-positive rate or ROC: the 'correct detections' percentage in Fig 8 is on merger-containing spectrograms only and the 20,000 merger-free test samples are not scored in the text. Detection only for three fixed mass points; RL error is averaged over all events without SNR or mass binning and uses a shorter 20-100 h merger spacing than real LISA rates. Fig 19 (Spritz time-to-merger errors) and Fig 18 not read quantitatively. Glitches and data gaps removed; no relay-node 8 h/day downlink.

models.title: Deep source separation of overlapping gravitational-wave signals and non-stationary noise artifacts
models.authors: Niklas Houba
models.venue: arXiv preprint (v2, 27 Jun 2025; no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF text read in full except the SBI pipeline figures; Figs 8, 10, 11, 14, 15 read visually).
models.architecture: Demucs-inspired encoder-decoder for blind source separation, ~2.79 M trainable parameters. Shared encoder: four 1D convolutions with ReLU (first three stride 2, so 8x temporal downsampling, features up to 512), a stride-1 bottleneck conv reducing channels 512 to 256 (no skip connections, no sequence compression). Three decoders (three ConvTranspose1D layers 256-128-64-c, kernel 8, stride 2): one for MBHBs (single channel, assumes at most one merger per window), one for the collective glitch stream (single channel), one for Galactic binaries with N_GB=5 channels (one per frequency bin). Loss: sum of MSE for MBHB, glitch and binned-GB targets. A downstream simulation-based inference (neural spline flows, sbi library) step is trained on separated MBHB waveforms for sky localisation.
models.inputs: Single TDI 2.0 channel (A, E or T processed independently by a shared model), 2 h snippets sampled at 5 s (1440 samples), simulated.
models.data: Simulated, 25,000 mixtures of 2 h: MBHBs from BBHx (IMRPhenomHM, masses 1e5-1e6 Msun, z=2-5, aligned spins), up to five Galactic binaries from FastGB (1-10 mHz, log-uniform, amplitudes 1e-22 to 2e-21; five 1.8 mHz bins), 0-30 Gaussian-burst glitches, stationary LISA noise. Test ensembles of 150,000 simulations for the MBHB and GB match studies; SBI trained on 50,000 examples.
models.training: Adam, lr 1e-3, 25 epochs, batch 16, ~4 h on an Apple M2 Max (PyTorch, MPS); unweighted sum of MSE terms (the author notes GBs are under-weighted).
models.results: Noise-weighted normalised match M between true and recovered waveform (TDI level): MBHB median M>0.95 above network SNR ~15 (median ~0.994 at SNR 50, 0.99+ above), steep rise from ~0.2 at SNR 5; glitch overlap with the MBHB barely changes M (median ~0.994 at SNR 50 across glitch offsets of -2 h to 0); GB median M>0.95 from SNR ~10 up to ~36, falling to ~0.65 at SNR 60 and ~0.3 at SNR 100 (out-of-distribution amplitudes). MBHB decoder 'hallucination area' 6.9e-5 (text) on glitch+noise-only data; example quiet segment: glitches M = 99.996%, GBs M = 77.753%. Inference takes seconds on a laptop. SBI on MBHB sky location is shown for two cases (no summary numbers).
models.code: No code or data link in the paper ('a few hundred lines of code'). GitHub searches found no repository belonging to this paper (TristanDonze/gb-sources-separation is by a different author on a different method).
models.gaps: Proof of concept with at most five GBs, one MBHB per window, Gaussian-burst glitches and stationary noise; no real LISA or LDC data; GB decoder cannot resolve overlapping sources within a bin. Detection FAR not defined: the MBHB-decoder power ECDF is the false-positive proxy. SBI comparison between separator-aware and truth-trained posteriors is qualitative. Figures 12, 13, 16-19 not extracted.

models.title: Decoding Long-duration Gravitational Waves from Binary Neutron Stars with Machine Learning: Parameter Estimation and Equations of State
models.authors: Qian Hu, Jessica Irwin, Qi Sun, Christopher Messenger, Lami Suleiman, Ik Siong Heng, John Veitch
models.venue: Astrophys. J. Lett. 987, L17 (2025); arXiv 2412.03454 (v2 dated 28 Jun 2025)
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF read in full; Fig 3 read visually).
models.architecture: Two conditional normalising flows. (1) Neural spline flow (96 M of ~160 M parameters per PE model) for 16-parameter BNS parameter estimation (coalescence phase marginalised), conditioned on a 128-dimensional compressed representation of the data from a learned embedding (MLP-ResNet; a Vision Transformer was cross-checked for the low-SNR band). The data are compressed by a custom multibanding scheme (~12 M points to ~6000 in 81 bands, 64 points per band), heterodyning with a perturbed chirp mass, and a 128-vector SVD basis (median mismatch ~1e-8). The heterodyning chirp mass is also fed to the flow. (2) A RealNVP flow infers a 12-dimensional EOS representation (plus maximum pressure/energy density hyper-parameters), compressed by a convolutional autoencoder, conditioned on (m1,m2,Lambda1,Lambda2); the autoencoder reconstructs the P-rho curve. Importance sampling (Dax et al. 2023) refines PE samples.
models.inputs: Simulated frequency-domain strain from one Einstein Telescope (ET-D, triangular, 3 streams at the Virgo site, counted as 3 of 5 data streams) and two 40 km Cosmic Explorers (CE2), 5-1024 Hz, hours-long BNS signals including Earth-rotation modulation of the antenna response; Gaussian noise.
models.data: On-the-fly simulation with IMRPhenomPv2_NRTidal. Two narrow priors: low SNR 20-50 (detector-frame chirp mass 2.0-2.1 Msun) and high SNR 200-500 (1.3-1.31 Msun); q 0.5-1, isotropic spins to 0.05, Lambda_tilde 0-1600, distance set by drawing SNR. 64 M waveforms (low SNR) and 100 M (high SNR). EOS training from the CUTER meta-model plus piecewise polytropes. Test: p-p test with 300 events per model; one network-SNR-35 event (1.74+1.56 Msun at 2500 Mpc) vs Bilby; EOS demos at network SNR 39 and 390.
models.training: Joint negative-log-likelihood training of embedding and flow for 2-3 weeks on one NVIDIA A100 per PE model; EOS flow trained separately (details in Hu 2024 thesis). Training inputs are on-the-fly noise realisations.
models.results: Posteriors agree with a Bilby+dynesty ground truth after importance sampling for the example SNR-35 event (initial flow samples differ in the tidal parameters; the example is called a bad case). Flow sampling takes <1 s on an RTX 3080Ti; importance sampling costs O(1)-O(10) CPU hours vs 3500 CPU hours for Bilby. Calibration: p-p test passes for all models, combined p-values 0.7805 (SNR 20-50 MLP-ResNet), 0.3303 (SNR 20-50 ViT) and 0.0782 (SNR 200-500 MLP-ResNet) with N=300 events each. EOS posterior recovers the injected pressure-density curve at network SNR 39 and 390 in under a second. The authors estimate a ~1000x (1/1000) reduction in total analysis cost without importance sampling and ~100x with it.
models.code: No code link in the paper. The first author's GitHub (MarinerQ) contains river, 'Parameter estimation for gravitational waves with machine learning', with multiband dataset, ViT/MLP/PCA embeddings and a CNF model; it is not cited in the paper (probable but unconfirmed implementation).
models.gaps: Gaussian noise and idealised ET+2CE network; no real or glitchy data. Only narrow chirp-mass priors (a model per band); 3500 CPU hours Bilby comparison is for a single event; p-p test only on 300 events and the SNR 200-500 model sits at p=0.078. No quantified posterior-width, KL/JS or ESS figures after importance sampling in the paper. High-frequency cutoff 1024 Hz and no free-spectral-range response.
models.is_ml_on_gw_detector_data: Yes (simulated third-generation detector data; parameter estimation, no detection)
models.adaptation_notes: 3G BNS NPE with multibanding.

models.title: MADGRAV: a multilevel anomaly-detection pipeline for gravitational-wave searches applied to LIGO data
models.authors: Gianluca Inguglia, Huw Haigh, Ulyana Dupletsa, Alessandro Longo
models.venue: arXiv preprint (IOP template, 30 Sep 2026; no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF text read through Section 6 and Appendix A; Figs 2-5 not viewed; Tables 1-3 read from extracted text).
models.architecture: Cascade of CNNs on 1 s Q-transform tiles (256 x 128, 5 Hz x 7.9 ms bins) of whitened H1 and L1 strain. (1) CAE anomaly detector (three conv blocks, 32/64/128 filters, BN, ReLU, dropout 0.2, max-pool with retained switch indices, over-complete 65,536-dimensional latent; mirrored max-unpool decoder; weak supervision with a margin loss that forces signal-injected tiles to reconstruct at least m times worse than noise). Per-detector reconstruction MSE is standardised to a significance sigma; trigger if network excess significance sigma_net>4. (2) Glitch-arm CNN (four conv blocks 16-128, GAP, 128-64-1 head, five-seed ensemble) scoring each detector tile, with Grad-CAM for timing. (3) Lag-maximised H1-L1 cross-correlation coherence statistic over +-11 ms. (4) A ridge/class-balanced logistic ln Lambda ranking statistic on seven features (sigma_H, sigma_L, coherence, two spectral centroids, two glitch-arm scores) with candidate floor ln Lambda>=4. (5) Two specialist CNNs (20-140 Hz and 50-500 Hz two-channel tiles) as gates; FAR from time-slide counting with an empirically measured calibration factor K.
models.inputs: 4 kHz GWOSC strain whitened against an ASD estimate; 4 s segments, central 2 s multi-resolution Q-transform (Q 4-64, 10-1291 Hz), central 1 s resampled to 256 x 128 and min-max normalised.
models.data: Training only on O3a: 32 of 143 coincident 4096 s blocks passing CAT1/CAT2 and no hardware-injection flag (36.4 h per detector; 131,008 tiles; 78,606/26,201/26,201 train/val/test; +-64 s excision around 7 known events); paired noise and bank-injected tiles from 102,400 IMRPhenomPv2 BBH waveforms (m1 10-120 Msun, q<=6, 100-5000 Mpc, network SNR 8-25). Specialist/glitch arms trained against real time-slid loud coincidences (O(10^3)) and IMRPhenomXPHM higher-mass bank (Mtot 100-400). Blind search over O3a, O3b, O4a, O4b H1-L1 coincident GWOSC data (725, 556, 818, 1086 segments = 106.8, 96.4, 125.6, 114.1 days; 442.9 days). Background: time slides, 266-623 yr per fold; injection campaigns of 122,850, 70,200, 58,500, 70,200 (O3a-O4b).
models.training: CAE: ten epochs unsupervised on O3a noise tiles then ten epochs of margin fine-tuning (Adam lr 1e-3, wd 1e-5, batch 64, plateau halving); frozen epoch chosen by validation injections above the 3-sigma point. Whole chain frozen after O3a training and applied unchanged to O3b, O4a, O4b.
models.results: 47 detections at calibrated FAR<1/yr with p_astro>0.9 (42 with p_astro>=0.99) of 48 candidates passing the raw threshold; 44 of the 47 shared with cWB; none without a catalogue counterpart; total masses 14-236 Msun (median 69), median SNR ~16. Recovered fraction of confident catalogue events rises with mass: for H1+L1 network SNR>10, 8.1% (<30 Msun), 39.8% (30-100) and 53.3% (>100), i.e. 33.3%, 45.5% and 53.3% of cWB detections in the same bins; over all 232 H1-L1 catalogue events: 5.6%, 20.3%, 24.2%, 33.3% in <30, 30-60, 60-100, >100 Msun. Injection recovery at FAR<1/yr reaches 50% near rho ~15-20 and plateaus at ~0.9-0.97 (Table 1). Sensitive volume-time peaks at Mtot ~100-130 Msun (O3: ~3.7 Gpc^3 yr; O3+O4: ~9.9 Gpc^3 yr) with volume-averaged efficiency 0.15/0.14/0.14/0.17. Relative to matched-filter pipelines and cWB the sensitivity is 0.2-0.5x below 100 Msun in O3 and 0.07-0.20x in O4, rising to ~0.5-1.3x at 100-160 Msun in O3a.
models.code: https://github.com/ginguglia/MADGRAV (MIT, created 2026-09-14, last push 2026-09-19): pipeline configuration plus trained CAE (assets/models/baseline_cae_weaksup_best.pt) and five glitch-arm seeds (lr_cascade/p1v42/arm_deploy_seed0-4.pt); specialist-network weights not seen in the file tree.
models.gaps: O3a is both the training period and a scanned foreground (32 of 143 O3a blocks used for training with only seven event excisions), so the O3a result and the time-slide background partly reuse training data. Efficiency of the pipeline at low mass (<30 Msun) is ~6-8%. Figs 2-6 (recovery maps, FAR vs mass, VT curves, ratios to cWB/matched filter) not extracted. The FARs include an empirical calibration factor K=1.43-5.60 (below), so the quoted 1/yr criterion is not a plain time-slide rank.

models.adaptation_notes: Multi-level autoencoder anomaly pipeline over O3-O4 with time slides and VT; long real-data runs.

models.title: Normalizing flows for density estimation in multi-detector gravitational-wave searches
models.authors: Sam Insley, Michael J. Williams, Rahul Dhurkunde, Ian Harry
models.venue: arXiv preprint (v2, 20 Aug 2026; no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF text read in full; Fig 3-7 and Appendix figures not viewed, Table III and IV read from extracted text).
models.architecture: Neural spline flows (glasflow/nflows; rational-quadratic spline coupling transforms; uniform multivariate latent distribution because time and phase delays are bounded) replacing PyCBC's pre-computed binned histograms of the signal density p(Omega|S) over inter-detector time delay, phase delay and amplitude ratio; dimension 3(N-1) for N detectors. 2-detector flow 4 transforms/10 neurons per layer, 3-detector 4/80, four-detector 128 neurons, five-detector 140 (Tables III-IV). The flow is used inside the PyCBC ranking statistic (pycbc_coinc_findtrigs) to evaluate the signal density of a trigger. It does not classify strain.
models.inputs: Per coincident trigger: relative arrival times, phase differences and amplitude ratios (one reference detector). Trained on simulated parameters, not on strain.
models.data: Training samples from a Monte-Carlo simulation of isotropic sky, polarisation, inclination signals (500,000 samples for the 2- and 3-detector flows; 700,000 for four, 1,000,000 for five detectors) with the paper's improved sampling (amplitude ratio, distance-driven SNR, measurement-uncertainty noise). Evaluation: PyCBC offline searches on one week of O3 (2020-02-07 17:49:37 to 2020-02-14 20:30:35 UTC) public LIGO+Virgo data with O4b-style ranking statistics, and an O4b-style search on simulated four-detector (LHVK) data with equal PSDs.
models.training: Adam, lr 0.001; training cost 0.25 (2-det), 1.25 (3-det), 3.25 (4-det), 8 CPU hours (5-det). Retraining is needed if relative detector sensitivities change.
models.results: Sensitivity at FAR<1/yr measured by injection recovery (O3, one week): the new sampling with the original histograms recovers 19 more injections (+0.55% of the non-HLV total); HL within 0.08%, HV +6.55%, LV +6.09%. Replacing the histograms by flows changes two-detector recoveries by <=0.05%; against the original methodology the flow search recovers 35 more injections (+0.78%) and HLV recoveries rise by 3.85%. Storage: histogram files 8.6 MB (2-det) and 2.1 GB (3-det) vs flows 59 KB and 1.2 MB (extrapolated TB-PB for 4-5 detectors vs <10 MB). Runtime of pycbc_coinc_findtrigs unchanged within 10%. First full four-detector PyCBC search: 511 injections recovered as four-detector coincidences, FAR range reported as 0.5 to 3.03e-4 (units missing).
models.code: No code or data statement found. Implementation is in PyCBC (github.com/gwastro/pycbc, GPL-3.0) with glasflow (uofgravity/glasflow, licence NOASSERTION); a GitHub code search found no flow code in pycbc, so the work may be unreleased or on a branch.
models.gaps: A ranking-statistic component, not an end-to-end ML detector. No trained model files released that were found. Fig 3-5 (recovery vs chirp mass; four-detector background/FAR distributions) and Appendix B density agreement not extracted. Sensitivity numbers are fractional changes of found injections (counts of injections not given), one week of O3 data, so statistical errors are not quoted. Four-detector test uses equal-PSD simulated data and has no baseline.
models.is_ml_on_gw_detector_data: Yes, with a caveat: the flow models a derived signal-parameter density (trained on simulated time/phase/amplitude samples) and is applied inside the PyCBC search on real O3 data; it does not consume strain.

models.title: Quantum Computing Tools for Fast Detection of Gravitational Waves in the Context of LISA Space Mission
models.authors: Maria-Catalina Isfan, Laurentiu-Ioan Caramete, Ana Caramete, Daniel Tonoiu, Alexandru Nicolin-Żaczek
models.venue: Classical and Quantum Gravity 42 (2025); arXiv v3 read
models.access: Open arXiv (2509.12929v3, 21 pp); PDF read in full, Figs. 10 and 14 viewed.
models.architecture: Variational quantum classifier (VQC) simulated classically with Qiskit: 4 qubits, first-order Pauli-Z expansion feature map (one input feature per qubit), Pauli Two-Design ansatz repeated 4 times (16 parameters per layer, 64 trainable parameters), all qubits measured in the computational basis, parity post-processing (Algorithm 1) giving a pair [P(merger), P(non-merger)]; COBYLA optimiser, binary cross-entropy loss. Hybrid pipeline: classical feature extraction and optimisation, quantum circuit for the model. Run only on local simulators.
models.inputs: Single TDI channel (A) windows of the Sangria series reduced to 4 hand-built features per window (spectral entropy, PSD mean, standard deviation, maximum; chosen from a list of nine), min-max normalised to [0,1]. Not detector strain: LISA simulated TDI data.
models.data: LISA Data Challenge 2a Sangria: one-year TDI time series sampled every 5 s (~6.3e6 points per channel), MBHB mergers only, Gaussian instrumental noise plus verification-binary, white-dwarf-binary and stochastic-background noise; training set has 15 injected MBHB mergers (noisy + clean traces), blind set has 6 mergers. Stage 1: ~1800 adjacent windows from each of train set, its isolated noise (train minus clean) and the blind set. Stage 2: ~63,000 overlapping windows from train and blind sets; a window is labelled 1 if it contains any point within ~4 days before to ~27 minutes after a merger peak. 50/50 train/predict split (Table 2).
models.training: Two-stage warm start: stage 1 trains the QNN to separate train-set windows (label 1) from noise windows (label 0) and to label the blind-set windows 1 (blind data used in training with label 1 by design); stage 2 initialises from stage 1 and trains on moving-window merger labels; ~170 COBYLA iterations; BCE; simulator only; threshold 0.44.
models.results: Stage 1: 1773 of 1802 blind-set windows labelled GW (98.4%), 29 labelled noise; no noise windows scored. Stage 2: 5 of 6 blind mergers detected at threshold 0.44 (peak probabilities ~0.465-0.75 over a baseline ~0.41-0.42); smallest-amplitude merger missed. A companion RNN (4.24M parameters, 6.3M samples) found 6/6. No FAR, no SNR-dependent efficiency.
models.code: No code link in the paper; no GitHub repo found by search (see code_repos). Sangria data public on Zenodo (LDC2a, Le Jeune and Babak 2022).
models.gaps: No false-alarm rate or noise-only test set; blind data used in stage-1 training; threshold tuned on unblinded truth; only one 1-yr realisation (15 train mergers, 6 test); feature-based (4 numbers per window) rather than waveform input; no latency measured (low-latency claim is asymptotic O(n_qubits N_samples)); simulator only.

models.title: Improving significance of binary black hole mergers in Advanced LIGO data using deep learning : Confirmation of GW151216
models.authors: Shreejit Jadhav, Nikhil Mukund, Bhooshan Gadre, Sanjit Mitra, Sheelu Abraham
models.access: Open arXiv (2010.08584v3, 10 pp); PDF read in full, Figs. 1-3 and Table I viewed.
models.architecture: InceptionV3 (316-layer DAG, ImageNet-pretrained), first 250 layers frozen; additional 40% dropout, a 1024-unit fully connected layer with Leaky-ReLU, and a new 17-way softmax head. Only P_CBC (the CBC-class softmax probability) is used downstream, by multiplying the H1 and L1 values and adding 2 ln(P_CBC,H P_CBC,L) to the squared PyCBC coincident ranking statistic: rho_ml^2 = rho_c^2 + 2 log P_c (MLStat). A post-matched-filter re-ranking classifier, not a stand-alone search.
models.inputs: 1 s of whitened, 16-512 Hz band-passed strain centred on a PyCBC trigger, converted to a continuous wavelet transform (analytic Morlet) scalogram saved as a grayscale image (3 identical channels) to feed the ImageNet network.
models.data: Training images from a manually curated subset of Gravity Spy glitch classes (15 glitch classes plus Power-Line split into PL1/PL2; 1080Lines, 1400Ripples, Violin Mode removed because of the 512 Hz cut, Koi Fish/No Glitch/Paired Doves/None of the Above dropped), plus a CBC class built by injecting SEOBNRv4 BBH (component masses 2-98 Msun, total <=100 Msun, chirp distance 5-300 Mpc) into real LIGO strain, and a Gaussian-noise class; 70/30 train/validation. Evaluation on PyCBC triggers from three chunks of O1/O2 offline data (~5.9, 5.3 and 5.1 days) with 5720 BBH+BNS injections.
models.training: Transfer learning with curriculum learning (three levels in the CBC class going from high to low SNR), SGD with momentum, checkpoints saved each epoch and the best by validation accuracy kept (plateau after 12th epoch of the last level). Training accuracy 100%, validation 95.8%. Framework not stated (layer count and 'DAG network' wording suggest MATLAB).
models.results: Validation confusion matrix: CBC class 98.1% recall (1.9% to GN); other classes 80-98.8%. ROC AUC 0.941 (0.8-5 Msun) and 0.973-0.981 (5-50 Msun). MLStat raises IFAR of GW151012 (5.84 to 218.1 yr), GW170729 (0.73 to 55.8 yr) and GW151216 (0.0173 to 1.453 yr, found as the top foreground of its chunk). Injection VT ratios 1.07-1.17 for chirp mass 0.8-5 Msun and ~1.2-1.36 for >5 Msun (stated as ~10% and ~30%). All GWTC-1 events PyCBC found are recovered (GW170818 absent from PyCBC). models.comparability_notes_extractor: Post-matched-filter coincident re-ranking on O1/O2 real data: IFAR gains and VT ratios are relative to PyCBC base statistic, not absolute sensitive distances; FAR/IFAR from time-slide backgrounds, so comparable with PyCBC/GstLAL-style FARs but not with per-segment FPR numbers.

Abstract says 'at least an order of magnitude improvement in IFAR'; the quoted numbers (37x, 76x, 84x) are consistent, but the GW151216 'clean detection' is IFAR 1.45 yr (FAR 0.69/yr), which is not a high-significance detection.
MLStat IFARs for events outside the three analysed 5-day chunks (most of Table I) rely on an assumption that the background reduction factor is constant across a run; they are inferred, not measured.

Injection study: the P_CBC classifier is trained on injections with SEOBNRv4 and tested on the same waveform family with chirp distance 5-300 Mpc into the same real data chunks; BNS injections lie outside the training range yet show a 7-17% VT gain, attributed to background reduction rather than classification.

Fig. 2 ROC FPR denominators are 'randomly chosen noise triggers' of an undisclosed number; no per-trigger rate is given. The ROC caption mentions the 0.8-5 bin AUC 0.941 despite injections outside training range.
Curated validation set (manual removal of hard images) inflates 95.8%/100% accuracy, as the authors acknowledge.

models.title: Novel neural-network architecture for continuous gravitational waves
models.authors: Prasanna M. Joshi, Reinhard Prix
models.access: Open access, Phys. Rev. D 108, 063021 (arXiv 2305.01057); PDF read in full, Figs. 2, 5, 6 and Tables I-IV viewed.
models.architecture: Shallow five-layer convolutional network designed for long CW signals (design principles: no pooling, combine all signal bins in the shortest pathway, daily-shifted spectrogram input): 1D conv with 64 kernels of 1x313x2 sliding along frequency per detector and segment (stride 16), 2D conv with 64 kernels 2x40x64 (stride (1,4)) combining neighbouring segments, flatten (16640), dense 32 (ReLU), single output unit with sigmoid (dropped when the output is used as a detection statistic). ~900k parameters; TensorFlow 2 / Keras.
models.inputs: Spectrogram of ten 1-day segments (1/day frequency resolution): real and imaginary parts of the FFT of each segment per detector (4 channels), a frequency window 1647 bins wide (18.7 mHz signal bandwidth for the widest case plus 16 bins padding each side) starting at the lowest signal frequency.
models.data: Simulated: stationary white Gaussian noise (H1+L1), 10 days from GPS 1200300463; ten targeted benchmark cases (five frequencies 20/100/200/500/1000 Hz x two sky positions, Sky-A easy and Sky-B hardest), spindown -1e-10 Hz/s, signals injected at the matched-filter D90% depth with random cos iota, psi, phi0; 8192 precomputed signals plus on-the-fly noise; separate validation and test sets.
models.training: One network per benchmark case, binary cross-entropy, Adam, batch size 128; each epoch uses all 8192 signal+noise samples and an equal number of pure-noise samples (noise regenerated every sample); validation every 100 epochs; training stops when validation p_det (p_fa=1%) >= 89%; ten random initialisations, best chosen; Weights and Biases tracking; NVIDIA A100 40 GB; 4-32 h per case.
models.results: Test p_det at p_fa=1% between 87.4% and 89.0% for all ten cases (mean ~88.3%) at the depth where matched filtering reaches 90% (D90% 86.2 / 81.8 per sqrt(Hz)); efficiency curve for Sky-B@1000 Hz follows the matched-filter curve; DNN statistic mapped to a chi^2 F-statistic distribution by a quadratic fit. Image-classification Inception-ResNet-v2 fails on the same problem except at 20 Hz.
models.code: No code link in the paper; no repository found (see code_repos).
models.gaps: Targeted (single-template), 10-day, Gaussian white-noise only; one network per case; no real data, no wide-parameter space; test set size not stated; no latency or cost comparison with matched filtering; ~1.7 point p_det deficit vs the 90% matched-filter figure; extension to longer durations and binaries left open.

The efficiency curve in Fig. 6 also lies slightly below the matched-filter line.
Fig. 5 'target' line is drawn at p_det=0.9, whereas training stops at validation p_det >= 0.89 (Sec. IV D); the stop criterion is therefore below the plotted target and cannot reach it.
Kernel width quoted as 313 bins corresponding to 3.4 mHz, but 313 bins at the 1/day resolution (11.57 microHz) is 3.62 mHz; the 3.4 mHz is probably the signal bandwidth and the kernel carries margin.
Test-set size and the number of noise samples defining the 1% false-alarm threshold are not stated; p_fa=1% is a per-sample fraction in a balanced signal/noise set, not a false-alarm rate in time.

models.title: Large-kernel Convolutional Neural Networks for Wide Parameter-Space Searches of Continuous Gravitational Waves
models.authors: Prasanna Mohan Joshi, Reinhard Prix
models.access: Open access, Phys. Rev. D 110, 124071 (arXiv 2408.07070); PDF read in full, Tables III, V, VI and Figs. 2-3 viewed.
models.architecture: Large-kernel CNN adapted from the targeted-search design of joshi2023: stem block of parallel 1D conv branches (kernel 1x14, 1x28, 1x42, 1x56, 64 channels each, stride 1x4) followed by parallel 2D conv branches (2x6, 2x12, 2x18, 2x24, with 1x1 channel reduction to 32, stride 2x4, 64 channels each), then three stages of two residual bottleneck blocks (1x1, 5x5, 1x1 conv, layer normalisation, channels 128/256/512 bottleneck, widths 512/1024/2048) interspersed with 2x2 stride-2 down-sampling convs, global average pooling, dense 64, single output (sigmoid for training, linear output as detection statistic). ~78 M parameters, ~300 MB per sample; TensorFlow 2 / Keras.
models.inputs: Spectrogram of 40 six-hour segments (1/6 h FFT resolution): real and imaginary STFT parts for H1 and L1 (4 channels), 824 frequency bins (~38 mHz, twice the widest 18.7 mHz signal bandwidth); search over wider bands done by sliding the window with half overlap.
models.data: Simulated: stationary white Gaussian noise (H1+L1), 10 days; six all-sky benchmarks (20, 100, 200, 500, 1000 Hz and one over 20-1000 Hz) and eight directed benchmarks (G347.3-0.5 at 20, 100, 200, 500, 1000 Hz; CasA at 20, 100, 200 Hz); 32,768 precomputed signals per case with random frequency shifts within the window as augmentation, injected at the WEAVE matched-filter D90% (rescaled to 10 days); an equal number of pure-noise samples, noise regenerated each step; independent validation and test sets.
models.training: One DNN per benchmark (14 DNNs): binary cross-entropy, Adam, batch size 256, validation every 50 epochs, early plateau by visual inspection, ~25 days per DNN on one NVIDIA A100 40 GB; Weights and Biases tracking. The p_fa used in training (0.76% per 38 mHz) is a naive estimate; final testing uses 0.48% per 38 mHz equivalent to 1% per 50 mHz.
models.results: p_det at p_fa=1% per 50 mHz at the matched-filter depth: all-sky 67.0%, 52.8%, 47.6%, 41.5%, 38.8% (20-1000 Hz) vs earlier DNN 60.5%, 24.5%, 11.2%, 3.3%, 0.7%; directed G347 72.7%-55.4% vs earlier 71.2% (20 Hz) and 2.6% (500 Hz); CasA 66.5-57.3% vs 54.6% (20 Hz). Sensitivity depths D90% 29.3 -> 18.3 /sqrt(Hz) all-sky (matched filter 39.0 -> 33.4). Single all-sky DNN over 20-1000 Hz: p_det ~36% average, second best at each frequency; full band search takes ~27 s of inference. DNNs not as sensitive as coherent matched filtering.

Single 20-1000 Hz DNN row of Table V is the 'average of p_det over frequencies calculated in Sec. IV C' (36.0%) at depths interpolated linearly from Table III, not at a single injection depth, which differs from the other rows.
The abstract reports 'high sensitivity at all frequencies' for the single DNN, but the p_det is 30-40% (Fig. 3) versus the matched-filter 90% at the same depths.

models.title: Transformer Networks for Continuous Gravitational-wave Searches
models.authors: Prasanna. M. Joshi, Reinhard Prix
models.access: Open access, Phys. Rev. D 112, 123052 (arXiv 2509.10912); PDF read in full, Figs. 1-4 and Tables II-IV viewed.
models.architecture: Standard vision transformer (ViT) on a stacked short-Fourier-transform (SFT) image: input image of consecutive 1800 s SFTs (time axis) by frequency bins, 4 channels (real/imag x H1/L1); image divided into rectangular patches (48x14 targeted, 2x4 directed and all-sky; patch height = twice the widest signal bandwidth in bins, half-overlap along frequency, none along time) giving 40/240/96 tokens; learnable linear embedding to 512, learnable 1D positional embedding, four transformer encoders (16 heads x 32, MLP 256, GELU), output block of global average pooling, dense 64 (GELU) and one output (sigmoid in training, linear output used as detection statistic). Same encoder for all benchmarks; TensorFlow 2 / Keras.
models.inputs: SFT image directly from standard 1800 s SFTs: 480x40 (targeted, 10 days, 22.2 mHz), 48x22 (directed, 1 day, 12.2 mHz) and 48x10 (all-sky, 1 day, 5.6 mHz) pixels in (time, frequency), 4 channels; the network slides binwise along frequency to cover the 50 mHz benchmark band.
models.data: Simulated: stationary white Gaussian noise (H1+L1). 26 benchmarks: ten 10-day targeted (Sky-A=CasA position, Sky-B widest bandwidth; 20/100/200/500/1000 Hz; fdot=-1e-10), ten 1-day directed (G347.3-0.5 and CasA; 50 mHz bands at the five reference frequencies, spindown from characteristic age 1600/330 yr, second spindown), six 1-day all-sky (five 50 mHz bands plus one over 20-1000 Hz); 8192 (targeted) or 32,768 (wide-parameter) precomputed signals injected at the F-statistic D90%, with equal numbers of noise-only inputs, independent noise per iteration, separate validation and test sets.
models.training: One ViT per benchmark: binary cross-entropy, Adam, lr 1e-4, batch size 256; validation every 10 epochs (targeted, early stop when validation p_det passes 91%, max 1 day) or 100 epochs (wide-parameter; fixed 3 days, no stopping criterion); one NVIDIA A100 40 GB; Weights and Biases. Detection threshold from pure-noise inputs (p_fa=1%); wide-parameter p_det uses the loudest statistic over the 50 mHz band, evaluated at the signal position and four neighbours for signal inputs.
models.results: Test p_det at the matched-filter depth: targeted 87.3-89.7% (Sky-A 88.9-89.7, Sky-B 87.3-89.3); directed G347 86.1-87.8%, CasA 84.8-88.7%; all-sky 88.3% (20 Hz) falling to 78.2% (1000 Hz). Sensitivity depths within ~1 /sqrt(Hz) of the F-statistic for directed and <~2 /sqrt(Hz) for all-sky (all-sky 1000 Hz ViT 11.1 vs F 12.8). A single all-sky ViT over 20-1000 Hz gives p_det ~0.70-0.79. ViT beats the earlier CNN at every reference frequency (qualitative). Sky maps at constant rho^2 show learned biases (p_det ~0.2-0.8).
models.code: No code link; data available from the authors on request; no repository found (see code_repos).
models.gaps: Only 1-day (wide-parameter) and 10-day (targeted) Gaussian white-noise benchmarks, no real data or lines, no binaries, spindown limited; 10-day wide-parameter case postponed; ViT still 1-12 points below 90% for wide-parameter searches; sky-position bias; training 3 days per network; not tested at realistic frequency-dependent noise; no code released.
models.is_ml_on_gw_detector_data: Yes (simulated H1/L1 Gaussian noise with injected continuous-wave signals, SFT inputs; no real detector data)
models.adaptation_notes: ViT on SFT images.

models.title: NNNN: Neural Networks for Newtonian Noise Mitigation at the Einstein Telescope
models.authors: Jan Kelleter, Patrick Schillings, Jonathan Kuckert, David Bertram, Markus Bachlechner, Achim Stahl et al.
models.venue: arXiv preprint (no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv (2606.19907v1, 18 pp); PDF read in full, Figs. 8 viewed; code repos inspected via public APIs (listing only).
models.architecture: Spatio-temporal network for predicting the Newtonian-noise (NN) force at a test mass from an array of seismometer channels: separate spatial and temporal convolutions inside a ConvBlock (temporal convolutions dilated 2-8), two ConvBlocks wrapped in a ReZero residual block (trainable scalar weight), two such SpatioTemporal ReZero blocks, then flatten and 1D convolutions producing the force time series. Spatial layers: 3x3x3x64 3D convolutions (memory-efficient variant for large arrays) for regular grids, or 4-head graph attention layers (GAT) with an inverse-distance adjacency matrix for irregular grids. LeakyReLU, dropout 0.4, Nadam, MAE loss. Compared to a Wiener filter (time-domain, trained on the same data) as benchmark.
models.inputs: 3 displacement channels (x,y,z) per seismometer, 100 time samples over 2 s, normalised to zero mean/unit variance, with white noise at SNR 15 added; 8 (regular cube 400 m or irregular optimised) or 32 (4x4x2) seismometers. Not detector strain: predicts the simulated NN force on one mirror along x.
models.data: Fully synthetic (no ET or LIGO data): own 3D simulation of P-wave and S-wave plane waves or Gaussian wave packets (frequency 1-10 Hz, width 0.5-2 Hz, amplitude 1-2e-9 m) in homogeneous rock, P-wave fraction 0.2, NN from the bulk integral (P waves) and from the cavern wall displacement (r=5 m cavern); validated against analytic Wiener-filter residuals. Three datasets of 1,000,000 events (80:10:10): single Gaussian wave packet, single plane wave, and sum of 10 plane waves (approximately stationary).
models.training: Trained separately per dataset and array configuration; MAE loss, Nadam, lr 1e-3 with factor-0.1 scheduler, batch 256; WF fitted by time-domain least squares on the training data. Hardware and training time not stated. Results evaluated on the 10% test set.
models.results: Stationary 10-plane-wave field: CNN and WF comparable (CNN residual <5%, ratios 1.1-1.4, ASD suppression 10-20). Dominant plane wave: CNN residual <20%, up to 40x better than WF, ASD suppression 10-40 (WF ~2). Gaussian wave packets, 8-seismometer cube: CNN residual 13%, 25-80x lower than WF, ASD suppression avg ~20 (30 at 1 Hz), WF <=1.6; 32 seismometers: CNN 9%, avg ASD suppression 25 (max ~50); GNN on regular grid 19% (avg 12), on an optimised irregular 8-sensor grid 16% (ratio 15-45, ASD suppression 9-16). Simulation validated against analytic residuals.
models.code: Simulation: github.com/lc316353/Newtonian-Noise-Simulation (exists, no licence file, last push 2026-01-28). Networks, simulation processing and Wiener filter: gitlab.git.nrw/jan.kelleter/nnnn (public, MIT, last commit 2026-06-10); no trained weights found in the repository tree.
models.gaps: Entirely synthetic homogeneous-medium P-wave model (no surface waves, reflections, mode conversion, layered geology), white seismometer noise, one test mass; benchmark is a non-adaptive Wiener filter (adaptive WF left to future work); no training-time, parameter counts or latency; no real seismometer or ET/LIGO strain data; GNN weaker than CNN.
models.is_ml_on_gw_detector_data: Yes (marginal: ML for gravitational-wave detector noise mitigation (Einstein Telescope Newtonian noise) trained on synthetic seismometer-array data and a simulated NN force, not on detector strain or real data; flagged for the caller to decide inclusion)
models.adaptation_notes: Seismic-array Newtonian-noise regression for ET; not strain.

models.comparability_notes_extractor: Residual (relative ASD of prediction error) and ASD suppression factors on synthetic NN datasets; comparable only with Wiener-filter NN-subtraction studies for ET on similar toy models, not with DeepClean-type strain-based subtraction or detection metrics.
suspected_errors_extracted: Sec. 5.1 refers to 'Fig. 8 (b)' for the stationary case ASDs; the stationary-case ASD panel is Fig. 6(b).

Abstract says CNN/GNN outperform the Wiener filter by 'factors of 15-80', but the text and captions give a WF/CNN residual ratio of 10-110 for the 32-seismometer case (Fig. 9), 'up to 40' for plane waves (Fig. 7), 25-80 for packets (Fig. 8) and 15-45 for GNN (Figs. 10, 11); and ASD reduction 'by factors of 10-30' while Fig. 9 gives an average of 25 and a max of ~50.

Stationary-case numbers differ between caption and text: Fig. 6 caption says both reach mitigation factors 'between 10 and 20' while the text says CNN 15-20 and WF 10-16; GNN ASD ratio 'as high as 15' (Fig. 10 caption) vs 'still as large as 12' (text).

The Wiener filter benchmark is a static (non-adaptive) filter fitted on the whole training set; the large advantage on dominant-event datasets partly reflects the non-stationarity of those datasets (single wave per event, direction and amplitude vary per event), not a weakness of Wiener filtering under adaptive operation; the authors state adaptive WFs are left to future work.

Dataset-mean residual (e.g. 13% for the CNN, Fig. 8a) is an event average of per-event relative residuals dominated by weak (low-RMS) events, whereas ASD suppression factors (e.g. ~20, i.e. 5% residual) are dataset-level ratios; the two summary numbers should not be compared directly.

models.title: External Attention Transformer: A Robust AI Model for Identifying Initial Eccentricity Signatures in Binary Black Hole Events in Simulated Advanced LIGO Data
models.authors: Elahe Khalouei, Cristiano G. Sabiu, Hyung Mok Lee, A. Gopakumar
models.venue: Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics 2025(10), 028; arXiv v2 read
models.access: Open arXiv (2506.03634v2, 16 pp); PDF read in full, Figs. 1-2 and Tables 1-2 viewed.
models.architecture: External-attention transformer (EANet, from the Keras example) converted from classification to regression: 256x256x2 spectrogram divided into 16x16 patches (embedding projection 128) passing through multi-head external attention (8 heads; learned external key and value memories M_k, M_v shared across samples), followed by two 3x3 conv layers (64 and 128 filters, each with batch normalisation and max pooling), global average pooling and a dense output predicting two z-scored targets (eccentricity at 15 Hz and source-frame chirp mass); MSE loss. 1,840,450 parameters. A dense-only head was tried and was worse. Ten independently trained models; deep ensemble (no gain over single model).
models.inputs: Two-detector (H1, L1) Q-transform spectrograms of whitened (20-512 Hz band-pass) simulated strain in a [-10, +2] s window around merger, resized to 256x256, 2 channels, z-score normalised.
models.data: Simulated: SEOBNRv5EHM eccentric non-spinning BBH waveforms ((2,2) mode only), chirp mass 15-60 Msun, q 0.25-1, e at 15 Hz 0.001-0.35, dL 100-1500 Mpc, random sky, inclination, polarisation and initial phase, 4096 Hz; 30 s waveforms injected into 40 s of Gaussian noise coloured by the O4 LIGO design sensitivity; only network SNR>10 kept; 5000 events in each of six SNR bins (10-15, 15-20, 20-30, 30-40, 40-50, 50-60) = 30,000 samples; 80/20 train/test split and 20% of train for validation. No real data, no glitches, no noise-only samples.
models.training: MSE loss on the two z-scored targets; Adam lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4, batch 32, up to 500 epochs with early stopping (patience 15), lr halved on 10-epoch plateau; best epoch 136; NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2070 8 GB, <1 h; ten independent trainings.
models.results: Eccentricity: MAE 0.042-0.049 (RMSE 0.052-0.064) at SNR 10-20 and MAE 0.018-0.025 (RMSE 0.025-0.032) at SNR 20-60, across e15Hz 0.05-0.30. Chirp mass: MAE 0.80 to 2.88 Msun (RMSE 1.10 to 3.65) at low SNR and 0.48 to 1.64 Msun (RMSE 0.61 to 2.16) at high SNR for Mc 15-55 Msun. ~100 ms per event. Predictions for fixed (e,Mc) cluster within 1 sigma (empirical 68%) region; low-SNR eccentricity is pulled towards the mean. No real events analysed (planned for GW190521, GW200105).
models.code: No code link; no repository found by search (see code_repos). Built on the public Keras EANet example (keras.io/examples/vision/eanet).
models.gaps: Gaussian simulated noise only; (2,2) mode only, non-spinning; SNR>10 only (no detection, no noise class); validation loss far above training loss (overfitting); no calibration/coverage of uncertainty, only empirical contours and 10-model scatter; no comparison against a Bayesian or matched-filter eccentricity estimate on the same injections; no real-data test yet; weights and code not released.
models.is_ml_on_gw_detector_data: Yes (simulated O4-sensitivity H1/L1 Gaussian noise with eccentric BBH injections; no real detector data)
models.adaptation_notes: External-attention transformer for eccentricity.
models.effort_basis: rule from the tags' one-off efforts (any L or >= 3 M: L; any M or >= 4 S: M; else S; unread: -)

comparability.what_differs: Point regression in Gaussian O4 noise.
highlighted_errors: A large train/validation MSE gap (0.003 vs 0.11) is not discussed.

models.comparability_notes_extractor: Point-estimate regression errors (MAE/RMSE) of e15Hz and Mc on simulated O4-PSD Gaussian-noise injections with SNR 10-60; not comparable with posterior-based PE (coverage/p-p, KL) or detection metrics; chirp-mass errors comparable in spirit to CNN mass-regression papers only after normalising by SNR and range.
suspected_errors_extracted: Sec. 2.3 states the model was trained on '80% of the dataset (approximately 24,000 spectrograms) with an additional 20% of this subset used for validation', but Conclusions repeat '24,000 spectrograms, corresponding to the training dataset' with 20% of it used for validation, so only ~19,200 were used to fit; the ambiguity affects the quoted training-set size.

The eccentricity convention is mixed: the paper defines e at 15 Hz and trains on 0.001-0.35, but justifies the 0.05 reporting threshold by LVK sensitivity to e>0.05 at 10 Hz (Ref. [65]); an e15Hz of 0.05 corresponds to a larger e at 10 Hz.
Eq. (2.1) omits the 1/sqrt(d_k) scale in the self-attention softmax; the model name is given as 'AENet' in Sec. 2.1 but EANet [50] in the references and Sec. 2.3 footnotes.

Fig. 1: validation MSE ~0.11 vs training MSE ~0.003 (mixed-SNR validation set) shows a large train/validation gap that is not mentioned; the 'robust' claim in the title is supported only by Gaussian-noise test sets.

Tables 1-2 intervals are 95% over ten independently trained models (training-seed variability) on a single test set per bin of 100 events; they do not include test-sample statistical uncertainty or injection-recovery uncertainty and are not coverage statistics.

models.title: Application of Non-Linear Noise Regression in the Virgo Detector
models.authors: R. Weizmann Kiendrebeogo, Muhammed Saleem, Marie Anne Bizouard, Andy H. Y. Chen, Nelson Christensen, Chia-Jui Chou, Michael W. Coughlin, Kamiel Janssens, S. Zacharie Kam, Jean Koulidiati, Shu-Wei Yeh
models.access: Open arXiv and open-access PRD (CC BY 4.0); PDF read (pages 1-15 by text, figures not viewed).
models.architecture: DeepClean (Ormiston et al. 2020; Saleem et al. 2024): a symmetric 1-D convolutional autoencoder with four strided convolution layers down and four transpose-convolution layers up, batch normalisation and tanh after each layer, many witness-channel time series in, one noise-prediction time series out. Applied here in a layer-wise 'multitraining' scheme: 13 sequential band-limited DeepClean instances (15-20, 33-39, 55-65, 75-80, 98-110, 137-139, 142-162, 197-208, 247-252, 295-305, 345-355, 355-367, 395-415 Hz), each cleaning the output of the previous. Loss J_PSD = summed ratio of cleaned to raw strain PSD over the target band bins.
models.inputs: Normalised (zero mean, unit variance), band-passed witness channels (Virgo auxiliary sensors) cut into 8 s kernels with 7.75 s overlap (0.25 s stride); target is the h(t) strain channel (Hrec_hoft_raw_20000Hz). Up to 122 witness channels per band; 225 channels used overall (abstract).
models.data: Virgo O3b, 2020-02-07 16:19:27 to 2020-02-10 10:35:01 UTC (2 d 18 h 15 min; the BNS-range figure spans GPS 1265127585-1265352161). Witness channels selected by BruCo coherence > 0.5 occurring at least five times in Feb-Mar 2020. Injection test set: 3,200 BBH signals (LALSuite/Bilby, ISCO frequency in 15-415 Hz, 32 s apart, distance uniform 5-30 Mpc) in the real Virgo strain; 128 injections (one-at-a-time PE) and 60 (15-parameter PE) used for parameter estimation.
models.training: Trained per 4,096 s segment (1,024 and 2,048 s also tried, worse), 90%/10% train/validation, 30 epochs, batch 32 (about 512 steps per epoch, 16,353 kernels), hyperparameters as in Saleem et al. 2024, models retrained 'approximately once every 105 s of data' (see suspected_errors). The 142-162 Hz layer needs about 80 GB RAM for 4,096 s.
models.results: Nonlinear noise subtraction demonstrated on Virgo O3b: up to 1.3 Mpc (2.5%) BNS inspiral-range gain from the 13-layer multi-band cleaning, 0.4% from each of the 98-110 and 142-162 Hz bands alone; mean recovered matched-filter SNR of injected BBH rises 1.7% (sigma 4.1%) with 71.3% of 3,200 injections gaining SNR; an ablation without tanh activations fails to remove the sidebands around the 150 Hz line, which the authors read as evidence of nonlinear coupling; single-pass training on 122 channels beats the 8-group sequential scheme. PE p-p plots on 128 one-at-a-time injections improve after cleaning (combined KS p 3.5e-14 raw to 0.021) while 15-D PE on 60 injections shows no improvement (p about 2e-4 raw, 1e-4 cleaned).
models.code: https://github.com/weizmannk/Virgo-DeepClean (exists; AGPL-3.0; last commit 2026-08-26, last push 2026-10-01; configs, witness lists and Bilby posterior pickles; no trained network weights found in the 745-file tree). Underlying DeepClean code is separate (ML4GW). Data availability statement says data openly available [43] (the repo).
models.gaps: Single detector, single 2.7-day stretch with extensive coherence; no comparison against Wiener filtering or NonSENS on the same data; SNR gain is small and two-sided (28.5% of injections lose SNR); 15-D PE sample is small (60) and shows no improvement; retraining cadence unclear; no search-level or FAR-level evaluation; run range figures given without a stated baseline range (implied about 52 Mpc).

models.comparability_notes_extractor: Denoiser metrics are not comparable across papers: here BNS inspiral range (SNR-8 convention) gain and matched-filter SNR change on Virgo O3b real noise. Comparable only to other DeepClean results (Ormiston 2020, Saleem 2024 on LIGO) when range baselines and bands match; the LIGO papers quote band-limited subtraction, not total range.
suspected_errors_extracted: Text says 'models were retrained approximately once every 105 s of data' while each model is trained on 1,024-4,096 s segments and cleans 4,096 s chunks; a 105 s cadence is shorter than the training segment, so this is probably a typo for 10^5 s (or similar). The cadence is unrecoverable from the paper.

Sec. IV B states that subtracting a single band does not reliably raise the SNR, with injections gaining and losing SNR in roughly equal numbers, yet the same section reports 74.8% gaining for the 98-110 Hz band.

The p-p results are summarised as 'closely follow the diagonal ... well-calibrated and unbiased', but the stated cleaned combined KS p-values are 0.0212 (one-at-a-time) and 1e-4 (15-D), both below 0.05, and the dL p-value stays at 0.00585 (one-at-a-time); the 15-D result is not better than uncleaned (2e-4 vs 1e-4).
The 55-56 Hz band contribution (+0.51 Mpc) does not match any entry in the 13-band layer list (55-65 Hz).
Fig. 5 GPS span 1265127585-1265352161 is 224,576 s (2 d 14 h 56 min), shorter than the stated 2 d 18 h 15 min (238,500 s); probably a dropped last partial segment, not stated.
Abstract says 225 witness channels across 13 bands; the text lists 167 channels in 98-110 Hz and 122 in 142-162 Hz, which overlap, so the 225 total cannot be checked.

models.title: Application of Artificial Neural Network to Search for Gravitational-Wave Signals Associated with Short Gamma-Ray Bursts
models.authors: Kyungmin Kim, Ian W. Harry, Kari A. Hodge, Young-Min Kim, Chang-Hwan Lee, Hyun Kyu Lee, John J. Oh, Sang Hoon Oh, Edwin J. Son
models.access: Open arXiv (v2, 30 pages); PDF read (main text and appendices by text, Fig. 7 viewed).
models.architecture: Shallow multilayer perceptron (FANN library, iRPROP training): 10 input nodes, one hidden layer of 10 nodes, 1 output node, bias nodes, sigmoid activation with steepness 0.5, MSE loss. 100 independently initialised networks are trained per case and their output ranks are combined with a maximum-likelihood-ratio (MLR) statistic built from the signal and background rank distributions.
models.inputs: Ten features per trigger from the coherent CBC-GRB search pipeline (Harry and Fairhurst 2011): single-detector SNRs rho_H1, rho_L1, rho_V1; coherent SNR; coherent chi-squared; new SNR; coherent bank chi-squared; coherent auto-correlation chi-squared; component masses m1 and m2.
models.data: Two short GRBs seen by Swift with H1, L1 and V1 data in S5/VSR1 (GRB070714B, GRB070923); per GRB, off-source background triggers (1,944 s of data around a 6 s on-source window, about 6,000-7,000 triggers) and software-injection found triggers (about 2,000-3,000), with spinning TaylorT4 3.5PN injections: BNS (NS masses 1-3, Gaussian mean 1.4) and NS-BH (BH 2-25 Msun, mean 10) progenitors, spins NS [0,0.4], BH [0,0.98), inclination within a 10 deg cone, detector-dependent distance ranges. Round-robin split (M=10) into training and evaluation sets. 6 s mock on-source blocks from buffer segments (37 and 27 triggers) used as unknown-trigger tests.
models.training: Per case 100 trainings with random initial weights, stopped when MSE plateaus (final MSE 0.08 NS-BH, 0.06 BNS); evaluation by efficiency vs FAP (ROC) and by detection probability vs injected distance at FAP <= 0.1%. Input reduction by Pearson correlation and PCA did not change performance, so all 10 features are kept.
models.results: ANN with MLR raises classification efficiency at the minimum FAP by 5-10% (absolute) over the pipeline's detection statistic (read: about 0.56 vs 0.50, 0.665 vs 0.565, 0.63 vs 0.545, 0.74 vs 0.635 for the four cases); BNS cases do better than NS-BH. The 90%-detection distance at FAP<=0.1% rises from 23.9 to 24.5 Mpc (070714B NS-BH), 12.7 to 14.8 (070714B BNS), 28.1 to 28.5 (070923 NS-BH), 16.0 to 17.2 Mpc (070923 BNS). On mock on-source blocks, the loudest triggers have FAP 0.14-0.56, i.e. consistent with background.
models.code: No code link in the paper; GitHub keyword and code searches found no repository. Built on FANN (Nissen) and the LAL coherent pipeline.
models.gaps: Only two GRBs, one run, tiny training sets per GRB (trained separately per event), ROC floor of FAP about 1e-4 limited by background count (paper notes 5 sigma needs more background), no real on-source result beyond mock blocks, no comparison with other classifiers, no time-slide background beyond off-source data.
models.adaptation_notes: ANN on features of a coherent GRB-triggered CBC search.

The MLR is built from the rank distributions of the same signal and background samples that are then used to compute the ROC and the distance-efficiency curves; signals above the maximum background rank get infinite MLR. Whether the MLR distributions come from the training or evaluation samples is not clear, so the 5-10% gain may be optimistic.

Reported 90% distances (12.7-28.5 Mpc) are 3-5x larger than the earlier exclusion distances (3.2-7.9 Mpc) for the same GRBs; the paper states they are different quantities, but this means no like-for-like sensitivity gain against the published search can be read from the paper.
Efficiency gains of the ANN over the detection statistic (about 0.06-0.10 absolute at the ROC floor) come from only the very lowest FAP region; above FAP of about 0.1 the curves coincide (Fig. 7).

models.title: Ranking Candidate Signals with Machine Learning in Low-Latency Search for Gravitational-Waves from Compact Binary Mergers
models.authors: Kyungmin Kim, Tjonnie G. F. Li, Rico K. L. Lo, Surabhi Sachdev, Robin S. H. Yuen
models.access: Open arXiv; PDF read (13 pages; main text plus Fig. 1 viewed).
models.architecture: Two classifiers on tabular trigger features: a random forest (scikit-learn, hyperparameters by 3-fold GridSearchCV) and a fully connected neural network (TensorFlow, ReLU, batch normalisation, L2 regularisation, dropout, softmax cross-entropy; shallow or deep topology chosen empirically). Their output ranks r are converted to a log-likelihood ratio ln L = ln[p(r|signal)/p(r|noise)] via Gaussian-kernel density estimates (bandwidth 0.03) so they can be compared with GstLAL's ln L and plugged into its FAR/efficiency machinery.
models.inputs: Six features per coincident H1-L1 trigger (one model each for H1 and L1 triggers): SNR, chi-squared, two component masses, two spin magnitudes.
models.data: GstLAL offline run on O1 (about 2015-10-21 to 2015-12-03) with software injections mimicking GW150914 (signal class) and time-slide coincident triggers as noise class; train/test 75/25 (H1: 3,641 signal / 129,405 noise train, 1,220 / 43,129 test; L1: 3,623 / 129,423 train, 1,238 / 43,111 test).
models.training: Imbalanced classes kept deliberately; RF hyperparameters by GridSearchCV k=3 on accuracy; NN hyperparameters set empirically and identical across data; training takes a few hours on about 165,000 x 6 samples.
models.results: ROC and AUC on test triggers: RF 0.666 (H1), 0.689 (L1); NN 0.661, 0.684; GstLAL 0.633, 0.658 (AUC gain about 4-5%). At the lowest FPR (about 2.3e-5) ML TPR is 0.103-0.125 above GstLAL (about 0.29-0.30 vs 0.17-0.18). Converted to FAR via the GstLAL procedure, the sensitivity range at the lowest FAR (about 1e-11 Hz) is about 1.7 Gpc for ML vs 1.4 Gpc for GstLAL; evaluation of about 45,000 samples takes tens of ms.
models.code: No code link; GitHub searches found no repository.
models.gaps: Single mass region (GW150914-like injections only), O1 only, features restricted to six, no data-quality or glitch information, no end-to-end low-latency or live-data test, interpretability not addressed (authors say so), no uncertainty on AUC or TPR beyond binomial bands, noise from time-slides only.
models.adaptation_notes: Random forest / MLP ranking of GstLAL triggers.
models.effort_basis: rule from the tags' one-off efforts (any L or >= 3 M: L; any M or >= 4 S: M; else S; unread: -)

models.comparability_notes_extractor: Trigger-level ranking inside GstLAL; compare via TPR at FPR rather than FAR in Hz. FPR here is per noise trigger with floor 1/N (about 2.3e-5), and FAR in Hz is derived by a GstLAL-style conversion, so it is not a measured rate comparable with MLGWSC-1 FARs per year. Single-injection-population (GW150914-like) test.
suspected_errors_extracted: The abstract's 'about 10% improved efficiency at lower false positive rate about 2e-5' is an absolute TPR difference of 0.103-0.125 (a 60-70% relative gain), so it is easy to misread as a 10% relative gain.

Abstract says sensitivity enhanced by about 18% at about 1e-11 Hz FAR; the text's central ranges (1.7 vs 1.4 Gpc) give 21%, and a volume ratio would be about 80%; the definition of the 18% is unclear.

Possible information leak: the signal class is software injections around GW150914 while the noise class is time-slide triggers across the whole template bank, and masses and spins of the matched template are input features (not examined in the paper: the signal class is a narrow GW150914-like injection set, while the noise class is a template-bank-wide trigger set). The classifier can learn the injected-parameter prior versus the bank prior rather than signal versus noise; the paper does not test with a mass-matched noise class.

FAR of about 1e-11 Hz is obtained from an FPR floor of 1/N_noise with N about 43,000 triggers from a few weeks of time slides; the paper applies GstLAL's FAR correction but the number of independent noise samples limits the claim, so it sits at the edge of what the background supports.

Test set trigger counts are about 1,230 signal injections per detector; no confidence interval is given for AUC or TPR at the lowest FPR where there are only a handful of noise triggers above threshold.

models.title: Identification of Lensed Gravitational Waves with Deep Learning
models.authors: Kyungmin Kim, Joongoo Lee, Robin S. H. Yuen, Otto Akseli Hannuksela, Tjonnie G. F. Li
models.access: Open arXiv (18 pages); PDF read (text plus pages 6 and 9 viewed).
models.architecture: VGG-19-style CNN in PyTorch (appendix describes 10 convolutional layers with 3x3 filters and 1x1/2x2 max-pool stages, so a reduced VGG) used for two tasks: (a) classification of spectrograms into unlensed non-precessing (U_N), unlensed precessing (U_P) and lensed (L) classes, with softmax and cross-entropy; (b) regression of five parameters (source chirp mass, lens mass, z_S, z_L, source-position y) with a regression loss on min-max normalised targets.
models.inputs: Constant-Q transform spectrograms of noisy simulated signals, pixel values min-max normalised to [-1,1].
models.data: Simulated BBH waveforms with microlensing beating patterns (lens masses 1e3-1e5 Msun, point-mass and singular-isothermal-sphere lens models, geometric-optics amplification factor) added to Gaussian noise from the Advanced LIGO detuned-high-power PSD; optimal SNR 10-50; 45,000 spectrograms per class (L, U_N, U_P); split 80/10/10 training/development/evaluation (4,500 per class for evaluation). Priors log-uniform in masses, uniform elsewhere (Table 1). A separate validation set built from GWTC-2 population models.
models.training: Adam, batch 128, up to 100 epochs, learning rate halved on plateau, NVIDIA Tesla P40; same setup for classification and regression; a model per lens type (PM, SIS).
models.results: Classification: lensed samples classified correctly 98.31%/98.07% (PM, Case I/II) and 96.73%/96.93% (SIS); unlensed 98.8-99.4% correct against lensed; three-class (Case III) accuracy for U_N 85.4%, U_P 70.3% (PM) with most errors between the two unlensed classes, L stays at 98.07% (PM) / 96.53% (SIS). Regression: match 0.979 for source chirp mass down to 0.819 for z_L (PM). On population-model validation data accuracy drops to about 68% (PM) and 62% (SIS), which the authors attribute to prior mismatch. Samples with time delay under 0.25 s are mostly misclassified.
models.code: No code link and no data link; GitHub searches (title, author topic, arXiv id) found no repository.
models.gaps: Simulated Gaussian-noise only, optimal SNR (no noise-realisation matched filter SNR), PSD fixed; no real data; no ROC or FAR; population prior mismatch lowers accuracy sharply; Table 4/3 y-column values partly ambiguous in extraction.
models.adaptation_notes: Lensing classification and regression on CQT images.
models.effort_basis: rule from the tags' one-off efforts (any L or >= 3 M: L; any M or >= 4 S: M; else S; unread: -)

models.comparability_notes_extractor: Classification accuracy/recall on balanced simulated data with optimal SNR 10-50 and a fixed PSD: not comparable to FAR-based detection metrics. Regression uses distribution overlap (M) and D_KL between predicted and true parameter distributions, not per-event error or posterior coverage.
suspected_errors_extracted: Sec. 4.2 says the proportion of correctly classified lensed samples in Case III is 'reduced by only 0.4%' relative to Cases I and II; Fig. 5 gives 98.31 to 98.07 (0.24) for PM and 96.73 to 96.53 (0.20) for SIS (relative to Case II: 0.00 and -0.4 for SIS), so the quoted 0.4% only matches SIS Case II.
Model is called VGG-19 (16 conv + 3 FC layers) but Appendix A.1 lists 10 convolutional layers; the architecture is a reduced VGG, not VGG-19 as named.

M and D_KL compare the marginal distributions of predicted and true parameters over the test set (KDE overlap), not per-sample accuracy; a model predicting the prior mean with right spread would score well, so M of 0.8-0.98 is a weak accuracy statement.

Optimal SNR (not matched-filter SNR in noise) is used for the 10-50 selection, and the validation data (12 < SNR <= 13) show accuracy of only 62-68%, so the 98% headline is not representative of realistic populations; the authors acknowledge this.

models.title: Deep Learning-based Search for Microlensing Signature from Binary Black Hole Events in GWTC-1 and -2
models.authors: Kyungmin Kim, Joongoo Lee, Otto A. Hannuksela, Tjonnie G. F. Li
models.access: Open arXiv; PDF read (14 pages, text only).
models.architecture: Ensemble of 10 VGG-19 binary classifiers (PyTorch; lensed vs unlensed), differing only in random seed, each outputting a softmax probability r of the lensed class. A hierarchical scheme (Fig. 1) makes an initial class per learner and detector with thresholds, a temporary class per detector by majority voting (with a reserved class R for follow-up), a primary class by detector consistency, and a final class using the median probability, its 90% bootstrap interval and an empirical p-value model.
models.inputs: Constant-Q transform spectrograms (20-350 Hz, Q=16, time step 1/256 s) in a [-0.9 s, +0.1 s] window around the event time, min-max normalised to [-1,1].
models.data: Training: simulated unlensed (IMRPhenomPv2 non-precessing) and point-mass-lens geometric-optics lensed BBH signals, lens mass 1e3-1e5 Msun, thin-lens approximation, injected into design-sensitivity aLIGO PSD noise with network S/N 10-50; 45,000 per class, split 80/10/10. Evaluation: 46 BBH events of GWTC-1 and GWTC-2, 32 s strain at 4,096 Hz from GWOSC.

models.title: Unsupervised Deep Learning Method for Clustering KAGRA O3GK Transient Noise Data
models.authors: Yubin Kim, Kihyun Jung, Kyujin Kwak
models.access: Open arXiv (12 pages); PDF read (text plus page 9 viewed).
models.architecture: Three unsupervised pipelines compared: (A) PCA (50-d) + k-means; (B) convolutional autoencoder (ConvAE, 4x224x224 input, symmetric conv/upsampling stack with batch norm and ReLU, sigmoid output, 64-d latent, Table 5) then PCA to 50-d and k-means; (C) Deep Embedded Clustering (DEC): the same ConvAE pretrained, centroids initialised by k-means on the 64-d latent, then encoder and centroids jointly fine-tuned with KL(P||Q) with a Student-t soft assignment. K=7 in all cases; t-SNE only for visualisation.
models.inputs: Greyscale Q-transform spectrograms of the main channel (K1:DAC-STRAIN_C20) cropped to 540x624 and resized to 224x224, four time scales (0.5, 1, 2, 4 s) stacked as 4 channels centred on the glitch.
models.data: KAGRA O3GK (7-21 April 2020, joint with GEO600): 2,531 Hveto-vetoed main-channel glitches (Omicron triggers, SNR>8, 28 auxiliary channels) manually grouped into six classes (blip, dot, helix, line, scattered light, scratchy) plus 'not classified'; 316 events at data-quality-flag boundaries removed, leaving 2,215; stratified split 70/10/20 train/validation/test. Labels used only for post-hoc NMI/ARI.
models.training: ConvAE: batch 32, Adam LR 1e-3, 50 epochs, batch norm after each conv, SSIM shown for reconstructions (Fig. 5); DEC: convergence at epoch 100. No seeds, repeats or variance reported.
models.results: On the test set, DEC gives the best silhouette (0.304 vs 0.050 and 0.010) and best NMI (0.367), while ConvAE+PCA+k-means gives the best ARI (0.436 vs DEC 0.298 and PCA 0.171). Deep features beat PCA on every external metric. PCA keeps only 31.3% of variance in 50 components. Line and scratchy glitches disperse across clusters.
models.code: No code link or data-availability code statement; only the GWOSC strain URL for O3GK is given (auxiliary-channel data not public).
models.gaps: Single dataset of about 2,200 events with heavy class imbalance, a single run per method, silhouette computed in different feature spaces, no comparison with Gravity Spy-style supervised results or other unsupervised glitch pipelines (the authors cite Oshino 2025 on the same data), class counts per split only in Table 1 (lost in text extraction).

models.title: Swift sky localization of gravitational waves using deep learning seeded importance sampling
models.authors: Alex Kolmus, Gregory Baltus, Justin Janquart, Twan van Laarhoven, Sarah Caudill, Tom Heskes
models.access: Open arXiv (12 pages); PDF read (text plus Fig. 2-3 page viewed).
models.architecture: Multi-headed 1-D CNN (convolutional feature extractor with MaxPool1d, BatchNorm1d, leaky ReLU, dilation) with three heads: a von Mises-Fisher (VMF) distribution on the sky (a mixture where multimodal), and Gaussian distributions for the two masses; its sample distribution is the proposal for importance sampling: samples drawn from the network are reweighted by likelihood x prior / proposal, with the likelihood computed from the whitened data, so the reweighted samples converge to the exact Bayesian posterior; effective-sample-size efficiency flags poor proposals.
models.inputs: Whitened and noise-normalised time series from H, L and V (2 s segments, 20-2048 Hz frequency-domain waveform then inverse FT), mass targets pre-processed to reduce their disparity (sentence truncated in the extraction).
models.data: Generated on the fly: precessing quasi-circular BBH, IMRPhenomPv2, prior in Table I, distance 1,000 Mpc rescaled to a target optimal SNR drawn from a scaled Beta distribution peaking at 15; Gaussian noise from design-sensitivity PSDs (aLIGO, AdV); a unique dataset every epoch.
models.training: 300 epochs, batch 128, 500,000 fresh samples per epoch, cosine-annealed LR, weight decay 1e-6; test set of 100,000 pairs at fixed SNRs; importance sampling tested on 100 zero-spin test strains at SNR 10, 15, 20 against Bilby.
models.results: NN alone: mean sky error 32 deg at SNR 10, 14 deg at SNR 15, 9.5 deg at SNR 20 (does not tend to zero at high SNR, about 6 deg at SNR 50); 90% area from about 3,000 deg^2 (SNR 10) to about 470 deg^2 (SNR 20). Importance sampling brings the best-sample error to about 15, 9 and 6 deg after 50,000 samples against Bilby's 1-8 deg; only about 30% of runs converge well; skymaps in about 5 minutes versus 3+ hours for Bilby, the essentials in 1-4% of Bilby's run time; poor proposals can be flagged by low sampling efficiency.
models.code: https://github.com/akolmus/swiftsky (exists; no licence file; last commit 2021-10-22; training, importance-sampling and evaluation scripts, noise curves; no trained weights in the 20-file tree).
models.gaps: Proof of concept: simulated Gaussian noise only, one noise realisation per event, 100 test strains for the importance-sampling study, zero-spin restriction to limit Bilby time, only sky and two masses, no p-p or coverage test of the final posterior, a VMF proposal is a poor fit to multimodal skies, low convergence at low SNR.
