models.title: Assessment of normalizing flows for parameter estimation on time-frequency representations of gravitational-wave data
models.authors: Daniel Lanchares, Osvaldo Gramaxo Freitas, Lysiane Mornas, Jose A. Font, Joaquin Gonzalez-Nuevo, Luigi Toffolatti, Pietro Vischia
models.access: Open arXiv (15 pages); PDF read (text only; figures not viewed).
models.architecture: GP15: ResNet-18 embedder that maps a stacked three-channel spectrogram image (H1, L1, V1) to a feature vector, conditioning a normalising flow (rational-quadratic coupling transform, masked affine autoregressive transform, then random permutation + LULinear transforms; nflows, PyTorch) that outputs posteriors over 15 BBH parameters (detector-frame chirp mass, mass ratio, two spin magnitudes and tilts, phi_JL, phi_12, dL, theta_JN, RA, Dec, phase, polarisation, tc).
models.inputs: Constant-Q spectrograms (gwpy) of the whitened strain from each of three detectors, resampled to 170x90 pixel three-channel 8-bit images (one detector per colour channel).
models.data: Six-second Gaussian-noise samples coloured with a pool of PSDs measured from four 500 s real O3 segments per detector, with IMRPhenomXPHM BBH injections accepted if network SNR is in 8-60; priors in Table I (detector-frame Mc >= 15 Msun, dL up to a limit that is doubled in stage 3). 3 million training images (10% validation), plus 3 million more with doubled dL limit for stage 3. Tested on 33 three-detector GWTC-2.1 and GWTC-3 events.
models.training: Three-stage Adam training, cosine annealing: stage 1 up to LR 2e-5 for 15 epochs, stage 2 anneal to 0 over 15 epochs, stage 3 15 epochs on the new dL dataset with LR 1.5e-5 to 0; NLL loss; 36 h per stage on an A100; no noise conditioning.
models.results: Injection p-p test (500 injections) has combined p = 0.54. Against LVK posteriors on 33 real events, spin, distance, phase and polarisation have JSD about 1e-3-1e-2, the mass ratio agrees across events, chirp mass is worst for events with Mc near the 15 Msun prior edge, sky position (right ascension) is the poorest; the model fails on events where the catalogue posterior is a single mode in inclination (GW190701, GW200129). Sampling 10,000 posterior samples takes 1.13 s on an A100.
models.code: https://github.com/Daniel-Lanchares/dtempest (exists; no licence file; last commit 2026-04-09; 'dtempest NPE library' with core and GW packages and examples; no trained weights found in the 60-file tree).

models.title: Denoising gravitational wave with deep learning in the time-frequency domain
models.authors: Yi-De Lee, Hwei-Jang Yo
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF read in full, 34 pp: text plus Figs 5-8 viewed as rendered pages).
models.architecture: Two-stage CNN denoiser in the STFT domain, 7,831,011 trainable parameters (2,198,225 amplitude autoencoder + 5,632,786 'Griffin-Lim network'; the two sum correctly). Stage 1, amplitude autoencoder: 2-D conv encoder-decoder on the 32x64 amplitude spectrogram (compressed 32x64 -> 16x32 -> 8x16, filters 64/32/16 then back), 7x7 kernels dilated by powers of 2, ReLU, skip connections. Stage 2, Griffin-Lim network: the denoised amplitude is thresholded by a sigmoid 'amplitude mask' (a sigmoid approximating an element-wise Heaviside step, parameters set empirically and not trainable) and multiplied onto the noisy real/imaginary spectrogram (the 'GL mask' of Eq. 1, eps=1e-8) so that the network only has to fix the phase; separate 'phase alignment' blocks for real and imaginary parts (SeLU, skip after every activation, dilations 1,2,4) and a 'cross-adjustment' block (2-channel complex input), three iterations; the final output assigns the denoised amplitude to the aligned phase and an inverse STFT returns the waveform. No numerical Griffin-Lim iteration is run: the algorithm only inspires the amplitude/phase split.
models.inputs: Whitened, normalised 1-s segment (2-s mock event whitened by a PSD averaged over 5000 noise-only sets, then 0.5 s cropped at each end) turned into a complex STFT with 32 frequency bins x 64 time slices, low-passed with a Hanning window (text says above 512 Hz removed). Single detector (LIGO Hanford). Target is the un-whitened simulated waveform in the same STFT representation.
models.data: Noise: real LIGO Hanford O3a strain from GWOSC, 2-s segments, glitches excluded (80,000 noise segments). Signals: SEOBNRv4 (PyCBC) at 8192 Hz, BBH only, m1>m2 in 5-75 Msun (total mass restricted to > 30 Msun in the abstract), no spins or inclination varied (mass-only parameterisation), 90,600 waveforms; only the last second incl. merger kept, Tukey-tapered and injected so the merger lies at 1.2-1.43 s of the 2-s segment (0.70-0.93 s after cropping). Amplitude set by a scaling ratio 0.001-0.045 (SNR roughly 4-12 per text; curriculum starts at 0.06-0.08). Every example contains exactly one signal; no pure-noise examples. Test set: 14,399 mock events, masses 4.5-82.6 Msun, SNR 4-25 (about 74% below SNR 10). Real events: GWOSC BBH events in H1 with SEOBNRv4_opt / SEOBNRv4PHM / SEOBNRv5PHM best-fit templates as references, from O3a (training epoch) and, for curiosity, O1, O2 and O4 (GW150914-v3, GW231231_154016, GW250114_082203 etc.).
models.training: Transfer + curriculum learning: amplitude autoencoder trained first (100 epochs curriculum decreasing the scaling-ratio range 0.06-0.08 -> 0.001-0.045, then 300 more epochs), then frozen, and the Griffin-Lim network trained 400 epochs on the same data; 30,000 fresh injections per epoch (random amplitude and noise segment). RMSE loss (amplitude stage); real+imaginary loss under the amplitude mask (phase stage). Adam with learning rate reduced at plateau. TensorFlow, 8x NVIDIA Tesla V100, about 1 day.
models.results: Mock events: 10,681 of 14,399 (74%) have overlap > 0.8 with the clean waveform; 6,612 of those (62%) have SNR > 8; high-SNR events are almost all recovered, low-SNR broad scatter (Fig. 5b). Best-case examples (Fig. 6, chosen with high overlap) 0.971-0.993 for total masses 35-130 Msun; performance is lower for heavier systems and the early inspiral is worst, merger best. Real events: qualitative only; denoised waveforms agree with best-fit templates around the merger for hand-picked 'ideal match' O3a events (Fig. 7) and for O1/O2/O4 events (Fig. 8); no overlap numbers, no per-event table, no event-selection rate is reported.
models.code: No code, weights or data link in the paper (PDF text search for github/zenodo/code found only the PyCBC Zenodo citation). GitHub keyword searches (denoising + Griffin-Lim; author name) returned nothing relevant (non-exhaustive; GitHub API rate limit hit part-way through the session).
models.gaps: Only signal-containing segments (signal location fixed within 0.23 s), so no FAR/efficiency, no pure-noise or glitch test; single detector; training SNR 4-12 versus test SNR up to 25; no baseline (e.g. Waveformer, WaveNet, Wei-Huerta) on the same set; real-event results are cherry-picked ('with ideal match') and unquantified; mass-only waveform model so spin/inclination are unmodelled; heavy-mass (low-frequency) events degraded by the preprocessing band-limit.
models.adaptation_notes: Time-frequency denoiser on O3a H1 noise.

Frequency band inconsistency: Sec. 2.1 says a Hanning window removes frequencies above 512 Hz, but Sec. 2.4 says the truncated part padded with zeros is 1024-4096 Hz.

Sec. 2.4 says 74% of SNR values fall below 10, described as the median SNR of the recorded BBH mergers; a median of 10 would put 50%, not 74%, below it, so the test SNR distribution is deliberately skewed low relative to real events (not flagged as such). The 74% of SNRs below 10 and the 74% of overlaps above 0.8 are unrelated numbers that happen to coincide.
Real-event panels (Figs. 7-8) are described as 'with ideal match', i.e. selected on the outcome; no number of tried events is given.

models.title: Cross-Temporal Spectrogram Autoencoder (CTSAE): Unsupervised Dimensionality Reduction for Clustering Gravitational Wave Glitches
models.authors: Yi Li, Yunan Wu, Aggelos K. Katsaggelos
models.venue: CVPR Workshops 2024 (per the authors' repository README; arXiv record has no journal reference)
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF read in full, 10 pp; tables extracted as text).
models.architecture: Four-branch convolutional-ViT autoencoder. Each branch is a CNN-ViT encoder (13 CNN-ViT blocks: two ResNet bottleneck layers + self-attention, with a 1x1-conv/avg-pool down-sampling module and an up-sampling module exchanging features between the CNN and attention streams, Conformer-style), embedding size 384 in the encoder and 192 in the decoder; feature maps pooled to 4x4 and flattened to a latent z_i per branch. A shared learnable CLS token queries the patch tokens of all four branches ('CLS Fusion', shared q/k/v weights) before per-branch self-attention. The four branch vectors are concatenated, passed through a fully connected layer, concatenated with the CLS token and a second FC layer into one low-dimensional latent code that is shared by four mirrored decoders; loss is the sum of four MSE reconstruction losses. Decoders are dropped at inference; the latent code is clustered with K-Means.
models.inputs: Four Q-transform spectrograms per glitch (Gravity Spy durations 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 s), 480x575 resized to 224x224, normalised to [-1,1].
models.data: Gravity Spy O3 main-channel dataset, 41,745 glitches in 23 classes from H1 and L1 (text); Table 1 gives 29,146 train / 4,169 val / 8,340 test (70/10/20). Labels are never used in training, only to score clustering. Class imbalance is large (Chirp 51/7/15, Wandering Line 66/10/19, Helix 94/14/27 versus Scattered Light 2,729/390/780).
models.training: Unsupervised, MSE reconstruction, 200 epochs on 8 Tesla V100 GPUs, about 4 days; model chosen on validation set; K-Means (fixed seed) on the latent codes.
models.results: Clustering on the held-out test split: ARI 0.4091, NMI 0.6362 (Table 2). Beats DIRECT (ARI 0.2137, NMI 0.4281, the Gravity Spy production clustering) and VAT with 1% labels (0.4054/0.5963) but not VAT with 5% labels (0.5938/0.7011). Ablations (Table 3): single-branch CNN 0.2792/0.5464, ViT 0.1243/0.3139, CNN-ViT 0.3118/0.5647; four branches no fusion 0.3186/0.5691, all-attention fusion 0.3518/0.6170, CLS fusion 0.4091/0.6362; reconstruction MSE 0.0137 (lowest).
models.code: https://github.com/Zod-L/CTSAE (linked from the paper; Apache-2.0; last commit 2024-09-10; training/extraction scripts, no trained weights in the repository tree; needs the Gravity Spy pipeline to regenerate spectrograms).
models.gaps: Single run, no seeds/error bars, K-Means with the number of clusters not stated; ARI/NMI only (no purity, per-class or confusion analysis, no accuracy against the 23 labels); VAT and DIRECT were re-run by the authors on their split, not the published numbers; no code for dataset split list; paper title claims dimensionality reduction but no downstream classifier is trained.
models.adaptation_notes: Four-view spectrogram autoencoder clustering on Gravity Spy O3.

models.title: Extract non-Gaussian Features in Gravitational Wave Observation Data Using Self-Supervised Learning
models.authors: Yu-Chiung Lin, Albert K. H. Kong
models.venue: Phys. Rev. D 111, 063520 (2025) (journal reference inferred from the DOI 10.1103/PhysRevD.111.063520; arXiv v1 March 2024)
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF read in full, 41 pp; Fig. 3 viewed as a rendered page; Figs 4-6, 13-17 and appendix not read).
models.architecture: Blind-spot WaveNet self-supervised denoiser (Noise2Void / Laine et al. blind-spot idea): the input is time-reversed and stacked on the batch axis, passed through a causal convolution to 1,440 feature maps, 12 stacks of gated (tanh x sigmoid) dilated causal convolutions (kernel 3, dilations 1,2,4 cycling, 1x1 bottlenecks 1440->360->1440, residual + skip), skip sum -> ELU -> shift by one sample (the blind spot) -> the reversed half is un-reversed and concatenated on the feature axis -> three 1x1 convolutions (2880, 1440, 1) with ELU. Output is the cleaned strain (no waveform labels).
models.inputs: 2-s segments (4096 Hz) of PSD-whitened strain, standardised to zero mean and unit variance; loss computed on a Tukey-windowed (alpha 0.25) residual in the Fourier domain up to the 2048 Hz Nyquist, i.e. the Gaussian-noise log-likelihood of the whitened residual.
models.data: Training: 120k random 32-s segments of real H1/L1 O2 and O3 GWOSC strain (CBC_CAT3 quality flag, 4096 Hz), 8-10 simulated CBC signals injected per segment 3-5 s apart (BBH SEOBNRv4T/IMRPhenomD, NSBH TaylorT4/IMRPhenomBHNS, BNS TaylorT4; spinless; BH 3-75 Msun, NS 1.4-3 Msun, q<=10, f_low 15 Hz; optimal SNR 5-25 BBH, 10-35 NSBH/BNS), PSD estimated on 128 s around each segment. Injected signals are never stored as labels. Test: 512 2-s segments per optimal-SNR bin (0.5 steps; BBH 5-25, NSBH/BNS 8-35), one signal each at ~3/4 of the segment, same noise source; real events: GWTC O1-O3 events (32-s window, centre 2 s), glitch tests with three Gravity Spy O3b glitch classes (Blip, Scattered Light, Fast Scattering; 3 each, glitch SNR 7.5-15, confidence >0.95), early-warning injections (SNR 20-50) and 11 Vartanyan CCSN waveforms at 1 kpc (optimal SNR 10-40).
models.training: TensorFlow, Adamax, lr 3e-4 (cosine decay to 1e-6 over the last 20%), minibatch 8 of random 2-s crops, 0.5M minibatches, no validation set (loss monitored only), 8x RTX 3080, about 120 h.
models.results: Mean overlap with the injected template rises with SNR but with large scatter: BBH and NSBH ~0.75-0.8 (2-s window) and ~0.9 (0.25-s window around the peak) at the highest SNR; BNS far lower (about 0.5 at SNR 35). On real catalogue events (overlap in the 0.25-s window around the peak) 37.8% of H1, 48.81% of L1 and 4.35% of Virgo events exceed overlap 0.5; GW150914 0.82 (H1) / 0.84 (L1); GW170817 fails (0.03/0.00/0.00). The model also reproduces Blip glitch morphology, partly loses low-SNR scattered-light and fast-scattering glitches, extracts short CCSN waveforms (not trained on) at higher SNR, and extracts inspiral features about 2 s (BBH), 4 s (NSBH) and 6 s (BNS) before merger at SNR ~50 (overlap > 0.2).
models.code: No code link in the paper; GitHub keyword searches (blind-spot WaveNet, self-supervised gravitational wave, author names) found no matching repository (non-exhaustive; search rate limit reached part-way).
models.gaps: Not a detector: no noise-only/FAR analysis, overlap-only metric; no comparison to supervised denoisers on the same data; overlap uses the known template and a 0.25-s window picked around the reconstructed peak; PSD estimated from data containing the signal; CCSN figure (Fig. 17), early-detection overlaps (Figs 13-15) and per-chirp-mass plots (Figs 4-6) not extracted here.

models.title: Self-supervised learning for gravitational wave signal identification
models.authors: Hao-Yang Liu, Yu-Tong Wang
models.venue: arXiv preprint 2302.00295v2 (7 Sep 2023); no journal reference on arXiv
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF read in full, 11 pp; Figs 4-9 viewed as rendered pages).
models.architecture: 'GW twins': Barlow-Twins-style self-supervised pre-training. Two identical encoders (1-D CNN adapted from a ResNet-50 backbone, a GRU layer added and pooling reduced, final fully connected layers removed; 2048-d representation) followed by a projector of three linear layers of 8192 units (BN+ReLU after the first two), trained to make the cross-correlation matrix of the two embeddings the identity (invariance + lambda x redundancy-reduction, lambda = 5e-3). Net A sees the signal plus LISA-like noise, Net B the same signal plus Taiji-like noise (noise as the augmentation); standard BYOL augmentations (crop, resize, flip, jitter, grayscale, blur, solarise) are also listed for the pipeline. After pre-training both nets are frozen, their embeddings concatenated and one fully connected layer is trained for a binary signal/noise decision (7-8 epochs, 8 used).
models.inputs: Whitened (Tukey alpha=1/8) and [-1,1]-normalised time series of a TDI-X channel for a simulated MBHB signal plus synthetic LISA or Taiji Gaussian noise; embeddings of size 2048.
models.data: Simulated only: SEOBNRv4_opt massive black hole binaries (Mtot 1e6-1e8 Msun log-uniform, q 0.1-10, aligned spins +-0.99, random angles), projected on LISA and Taiji with the LDC-2 / Taiji mock-data-challenge noise models (PSDs from Eqs 3-5), TDI-1.0 / 1.5 / 2.0 generations, f 3e-5-0.05 Hz. Test sets: 10,000 signal and 10,000 noise-only samples; text gives SNR 30-50 and 'false alarm rate at 1%' for the test and SNR 20 for the data preparation. No real detector data.
models.training: Pre-training: LARS optimiser (AdamW lr 1e-4 also works), 1000 epochs, batch 2048, lr 0.2 weights / 0.0048 biases, 10 warm-up epochs then cosine decay by 1000x, lambda 5e-3. Downstream: FC layer on frozen embeddings, 8 epochs. Compute time stated only in Fig. 9 (units absent).
models.results: AUC 0.84-0.866 across TDI generations and epochs (Fig. 4; best 0.85271 for TDI-1.0, ~0.866 for TDI-2.0), accuracy 0.78-0.80, precision 0.84-0.90, recall 0.64-0.70, F1 0.745-0.775 (Figs 5-6). JS divergence between posteriors from different TDI generations is near-maximal for the masses (0.63-0.78) and ~1e-4-6e-4 for phase, inclination and polarisation (dingo-based PE, Figs 7-8). Relative run time SSL < LSTM < LDASoft (Fig. 9).

models.title: Classification of gravitational-wave glitches via dictionary learning
models.authors: Miquel Llorens-Monteagudo, Alejandro Torres-Forne, Jose A. Font, Antonio Marquina
models.venue: Class. Quantum Grav. (DOI 10.1088/1361-6382/ab0657); arXiv v1 9 Nov 2018 shows no journal reference
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF read in full, 19 pp; confusion-matrix Figs 8-11 viewed as rendered pages).
models.architecture: Sparse-coding / dictionary-learning classifier (a supervised-learning method but not a neural network). Phase 1 (denoising): three trained dictionaries, one per glitch morphology (sine-Gaussian SG: 512 atoms of 256 samples; Gaussian G: 256 atoms of 128; ring-down RD: 512 atoms of 256), learned with the Mairal online (mini-batch) algorithm and applied by LASSO / LARS with a single regularisation lambda_tr = 0.09 to give three 'parent' reconstructions per glitch. Phase 2 (classification): three untrained dictionaries (256 atoms each, atoms = whole centred ideal glitches of one morphology) reconstruct each parent with one non-zero coefficient (12 reconstructions in total per glitch); the predicted class is the dictionary whose children have the smallest product of DSSIM (structural dissimilarity) to their parents.
models.inputs: One 16384-sample (1 s at 16384 Hz) simulated glitch embedded in coloured Gaussian noise (advanced LIGO broadband PSD); denoising dictionaries trained on patches (20,000 per dictionary) of the L2-normalised glitches.
models.data: Fully synthetic: SG, G and RD glitches (f0 40-1500 Hz, hrss 5e-22-4e-21, Q 2-20 for SG/RD, duration 1-10 ms for G; parameters log-uniform; following the pipelines of reference [9]), injected into Gaussian noise coloured by the Advanced LIGO design (broadband) PSD. Training sets 915 SG, 62,440 G and 603 RD glitches; 300 validation glitches (100/class) for tuning; final test 3000 glitches (1000/class) with SNR uniform in 1-400 (validation runs at SNR 20). No real LIGO glitches.
models.training: Dictionary learning (Mairal et al.) with lambda_learn 0.02 (SG), 0.006 (G), 0.01 (RD); LARS/LASSO reconstruction; hyper-parameters (atom length, atom count, lambda_tr, number of non-zero coefficients, number of classification atoms) tuned on 300 validation glitches by confusion matrix. Reconstructing 3000 glitches by the three dictionaries took about 36 h on an AMD Phenom II x4 with 12 GB RAM.
models.results: Final test, 3000 simulated glitches: 2879 correct (96.0%): Gaussian 999/1000, SG 908 (92 wrong: 26 to G, 66 to RD), RD 972 (28 wrong: 21 to SG, 7 to G); no glitch lost. Validation (300 glitches, SNR 20) with the final settings: 296/300 (98.7%). Errors concentrate at SNR < 10 and at extreme frequencies.
models.code: No code or data link in the paper; GitHub keyword searches (dictionary learning glitch / denoising) found nothing (non-exhaustive).
models.gaps: Simulated glitch families only, loosely three morphologies, injected at known positions into Gaussian noise; no real Gravity Spy glitches; no trigger stage (noise or signals would also be classified); only accuracy/confusion matrices (no per-SNR quantification beyond histograms); very slow denoising (about 43 s per glitch).

models.title: Simulating Transient Noise Bursts in LIGO with Generative Adversarial Networks
models.authors: Melissa Lopez, Vincent Boudart, Kerwin Buijsman, Amit Reza, Sarah Caudill
models.venue: Phys. Rev. D 106, 023027 (2022) (journal reference inferred from the DOI); arXiv v1 shows no journal reference
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF read in full, 17 pp; Figs 8 and 9-11 viewed as rendered pages).
models.architecture: CT-GAN (Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty and consistency term), 1-D. Generator: 100-d latent vector -> NN-upsampling + conv (kernel 5, no padding) + BatchNorm + LeakyReLU(0.2) stages with 1024-512-256-128-64 channels, dilations 2,4,6,8,16, Tanh output of 938 samples. Discriminator: strided convolutions (64-128-256-512-1024-2048 channels) with spectral normalisation, dropout (rate 0.6, not on first/last layer, needed for the CT term) and LeakyReLU. lambda_GP = 5 and lambda_CT = 5.
models.inputs: Time-domain whitened blips, 938 samples at 4096 Hz (0.23 s), amplitude in [-1,1]; generator input is Gaussian latent noise.
models.data: Gravity Spy O2 blip glitches from L1 and H1 with confidence c_GS >= 0.9 (5540 L1, 6768 H1 listed in Table I); whitened locally with BayesLine, extracted from noise with BayesWave (wavelet reconstruction), smoothed with the regularised Rudin-Osher-Fatemi denoiser (lambda 0.5) to remove high-frequency BayesWave artefacts, re-injected into real whitened noise and kept only if Gravity Spy still gave c >= 0.9 twice. Final sets 3291 (L1) and 2587 (H1) blips (59% and 38% of the starting sets).
models.training: RMSProp, lr 1e-4, discriminator updated 5x per generator step, 500 epochs, one TITAN V GPU, about 7.75 h (text states 96 GB memory). Both losses stabilise by about epoch 100.
models.results: Generates about 1000 blips in about 5 s per detector. Gravity Spy classifies >70% of 1000 H1 fakes as Blip at every injected SNR tested, rising with SNR; Wasserstein distance, match and normalised cross-covariance between fake and real populations show a near-linear relation with Pearson coefficient 0.993-0.999 (Table II), taken as evidence that the distribution is learned. Similarity metrics also separate 'anomalous' generations that Gravity Spy mis-scores as Blip. Applications (PCA clustering, SVD glitch template bank with 10 basis vectors, mock-data injection into O3a data with ALBUS) shown as proofs of concept.
models.code: No code or data link in the paper; GitHub searches (LIGO glitch GAN, blip GAN, author name) found nothing (non-exhaustive).
models.gaps: Blips only; heavy preprocessing loses 34-62% of the data; no real-versus-generated classifier two-sample test; quality metrics are self-referential (generated vs generated compared with generated vs real; Gravity Spy is itself biased towards Blip); no downstream improvement of any search or classifier demonstrated.

models.title: Extraction of binary neutron star gravitational wave waveforms from Einstein Telescope using deep learning
models.authors: Cunliang Ma, Xinyao Yu, Zhoujian Cao, Mingzhen Jia
models.venue: arXiv preprint 2406.15813v1 (22 Jun 2024); no journal reference on arXiv
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF read in full, 14 pp; Figs 9-15 viewed as rendered pages).
models.architecture: Three band-specific denoisers plus three 'Amplitude Regularity' models, stitched into a full BNS waveform (SPIIR-inspired: each channel is delayed, low-pass filtered with a Butterworth filter, resampled, denoised and the denoised outputs summed). Denoising model: U-Net-like encoder-decoder (4 encoder blocks of residual conv + max-pool with filters 32-512 and kernels 64-16; 1 ResNet block; Bridge I; 3 Transformer blocks, 4 heads, dropout 0.1, MLP 128; Bridge II; 4 decoder blocks with skip connections) followed by a feed-forward conv head. Amplitude Regularity model: the same network with the Transformer and Bridge parts removed and pooling 4, trained to repair amplitude loss in the denoiser output. All three processes use inputs of 40,960 samples: Process I 512 Hz x 80 s (early inspiral), II 2048 Hz x 20 s (late inspiral), III 8192 Hz x 5 s (near merger). Waveform construction: spline-upsample to 8192 Hz, amplitude-match overlapping parts and blend with weights in the overlaps.
models.inputs: One ET detector's whitened-by-construction strain (ET PSD, EinsteinTelescopeP1600143), low-passed at 256 Hz / 1024 Hz and resampled for the early/late processes; 100-s BNS signals at 8192 Hz.
models.data: Synthetic only (PyCBC): IMRPhenomD_NRTidal, component masses 1-2 Msun, dimensionless spins 0-0.998, random sky position, nominal 100 Mpc then amplitude rescaled to a random SNR 20-40 (training) and 20-80 (test); noise coloured with the ET PSD (single detector). 30,000 packages, each one 256-s noise sample plus ten 100-s signals: 24,000 train, 3,000 validation, 3,000 test (30,000 test waveforms); training samples are synthesised on the fly (random signal, slide, SNR, noise slice).
models.training: Not given as a schedule (optimiser, learning rate, epochs and batch size are not stated in the text read). MSE loss between denoised and buried signal for the denoisers and between regularised and buried signal for the Amplitude Regularity models.
models.results: Overlap (Eq. 22, no time/phase maximisation, so it penalises phase and amplitude errors) of denoised output with the buried signal: early-inspiral segments, fraction of test samples with overlap > 0.9 rises from ~70% (U-Net without Transformer) to ~90% (with Transformer) to ~95% (with Amplitude Regularity model); example overlaps at SNR 20/40/60/80 improve from 0.797/0.974/0.988/0.993 (early), 0.916/0.985/0.995/0.996 (late), 0.948/0.980/0.990/0.993 (merger) and 0.863/0.979/0.990/0.994 (whole 100 s) to 0.940/0.989/0.995/0.997, 0.953/0.996/0.998/0.999, 0.967/0.984/0.992/0.995 and 0.933/0.990/0.995/0.997 after regularisation. Merger amplitude tends to be attenuated prematurely.

models.architecture: TasNet-style time-domain source separation applied to two overlapping GW signals plus noise, using a Dual-Path RNN (DPRNN; Conv-TasNet and DPTNet were also tried and DPRNN was best, no numbers given). Encoder: Conv1D with C=256 filters (size 2) + ReLU on the 4-s strain; Separation: LayerNorm + Conv1D to N=64 channels, segmentation into S=134 chunks of K=250 (50% overlap), four DPRNN blocks (intra-chunk BiLSTM, hidden 256, then inter-chunk BiLSTM, each with FC + LayerNorm + residual), Conv2D, overlap-add, parallel tanh/sigmoid gated convolutions and a ReLU producing two masks M_A, M_B; Decoder: transposed Conv1D (kernel 2, stride 1) back to one-channel waveforms.

models.training: Utterance-level permutation-invariant training maximising scale-invariant SNR (SI-SNR); Adam, lr 1e-5, 20 epochs. Hardware and time not stated.
models.results: A signal counts as separated when its overlap with the injected source is > 0.9. With peak-time difference 0 s (merger coincident), both signals are separated in ~83% of 1000 samples, only one in ~12%, neither in ~5%; with a 1-s difference ~97% are fully separated. With A at SNR 10, both signals separated in ~55% when B has SNR 6, ~87% at 8, ~95% at 10 and ~93% at 20 (the weaker signal fails more often at large SNR gaps). Single illustrative cases: both overlaps > 0.95 at zero time difference; B at SNR 6 only 0.82 overlap, which stays 0.80 when A is removed (noise-limited).

models.title: Matched filtering for gravitational wave detection without template bank driven by deep learning template prediction model bank
models.authors: CunLiang Ma, Sen Wang, Wei Wang, Zhoujian Cao
models.venue: Phys. Rev. D 109, 043009 (2024); arXiv v1 5 Sep 2023 (the authors later call the framework MSNRnet)
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF read in full, 20 pp; Figs 9 and the training-method page viewed as rendered pages).
models.architecture: Four-stage interpretable search: (1) significant-time prediction: a pre-trained U-Net envelope-extraction network (from the authors' earlier paper, ref [31]) run on each detector's whitened strain, a coalescence time is flagged when the predicted envelope exceeds 0.5 and the H1/L1 times agree within 0.05 s; (2) preliminary template prediction: a bank of 10 denoising U-Nets (the same structure, 11 layers), one per mass sub-space of (m1,m2) in (5,10],(10,20],(20,40],(40,80] with input durations 2.00 s down to 0.25 s (Table I); (3) template selection: 10 astrophysical-origin discrimination CNNs (Gabbard-style 1-D CNN, Table II: conv 32-32-64-64-128-128 with filters 32-32-16-16-8-8, dense 64/32/2, ELU, dropout 0.5) that accept a denoised output as a template when its score exceeds 0.5 in both detectors; (4) matched filtering of the selected predicted templates against the strain, network SNR = max over templates of sqrt(rho_H^2 + rho_L^2). For comparison the paper also trains 10 end-to-end sub-space classifiers (the P_score route) and a no-selection (PTP+MF only) variant.
models.inputs: Whitened strain (Weltch-estimated ASD) at 4096 Hz from H1 and L1; denoiser inputs are 0.25-2 s windows cut so that the envelope peak sits in the final 0.05 s.
models.data: Training data: 10 sub-space sets of 100,000 samples each; 16-s synthetic injections (IMRPhenomD when a component is < 10 Msun, otherwise SEOBNRv4; spins 0-0.998, random sky) added to real LIGO O3a background noise (GPS 1238163456-1238806528, 4096 Hz). The SNR is redrawn every batch from a staged schedule of ranges: (17-20), (14-17), (10-14), (5-10), (5-10), (10-14), (14-17); the signal merger falls within 60-95% of each window. 30 epochs, Adam 1.5e-5, batch 64. Discrimination data (10,000 positive + 10,000 negative per sub-space): positives are denoiser outputs whose overlap with the buried signal exceeds 0.8; negatives are (I) denoiser outputs for noise-only input, screened by hand, (II) denoiser outputs with overlap < 0.8, and (III) 9,080 outputs for noise segments that trigger the envelope network, taken from the first half of Aug 2017. Three APOD models (I, II, III) are trained on 20,000 / 40,000 / 58,160 samples (Adam 1.5e-5, batch 16). Test data: 10 simulated test sets of 10,000 samples each (background GPS 1238904832-1239023616, O3a), the confident events of GWTC-1/2/2.1/3, and the second half of the Aug 2017 (O2) run (GPS 1186683883-1187733597).
models.training: As above; the envelope model is reused. RTX 3060 Laptop (6 GB) is enough to train and run a denoiser (conclusion).
models.results: Denoiser overlap > 0.9 for >= 97.5% of samples in the heaviest class and ~60% in the lightest, clearly better than a single full-parameter denoiser; predicted template SNRs track true SNRs but are biased high (relative error positive); discrimination CNNs reject noise-only outputs. Simulated-test ROC (noise samples, FAP): TAP ~0.8 at FAP 1e-4 for Methods I-III in most sub-spaces versus ~0 for PTP+MF only and ~0.3-0.5 for the end-to-end classifiers. Real events: of 80 confident events analysed (Table IV) Method I recovers 57 (71%), II 48 (60%), III 33 (41%), network SNRs typically 7% above GstLAL; GW170608 denoised overlap 0.95 (2 s) / 0.99 (0.25 s). Second half of Aug 2017 (12.15 days): with H+L coincidence, time-difference (<13 ms) and network-SNR > 8 cuts there remain 28 false triggers (Method I), 2 (II) and 0 (III).
models.code: No code link in the paper; GitHub keyword searches (MSNRnet, template-free matched filtering with denoising, author name) found no repository (non-exhaustive).
models.gaps: False alarms are counted over only 12.15 days of one epoch (O2 Aug 2017) with a network trained on O3a noise and partly on first-half Aug 2017 data, so no FAR beyond ~1/12 per day can be set (zero-trigger result is an upper limit of ~90/yr at 95%); ROC FAP is per 0.25-2 s test sample over 10,000 noise samples (resolution 1e-4) and is not a per-time FAR; no comparison with any baseline detector at matched FAR; detection rate defined by the discriminator output, not p_astro; templates are not parameter-labelled.
models.adaptation_notes: Denoiser plus template-free matched filtering (MSNRnet).

models.title: Mitigating the impact of noise transients in gravitational-wave searches using reduced basis timeseries and convolutional neural networks
models.authors: Ryan Magee, Ritwik Sharma, Ananya Agrawal, Rhiannon Udall
models.venue: arXiv preprint (no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv; full PDF read (text extracted page by page; key figures and tables viewed as images).
models.architecture: Per-region binary CNN used as a signal-consistency veto on GstLAL matched-filter triggers. Input is the set of SVD-basis SNR responses Q_mu(t)=<u_mu|d> for a template-bank region, cut to 0.1 s around the peak and Fourier-transformed (real/imag components interleaved in alternate columns), giving a 37x402 (glitch-like bank) or 30x402 (LVK-consistent bank) single-channel greyscale image. Network (Table I): Conv2D 16 filters 7x7 -> MaxPool 2x2 -> Conv2D 32 filters 7x7 -> MaxPool 2x2 -> Dense 16 -> 1 sigmoid, Leaky ReLU after each pooling layer; roughly tens of thousands of weights. Output p_signal; p_glitch=1-p_signal. A modified toy ranking statistic rho_bar weights the xi^2 consistency term by (2 p_glitch+1)/2 (factor in [0.5,1.5]), so a poor classifier can change xi^2 by at most 2x. 12 independent classifiers per bank (4 glitch scenarios x 3 signal scenarios).
models.inputs: Single-detector basis-response images (frequency domain), one per candidate; not strain. Glitch-like bank: 234 IMRPhenomD templates, 10-100 Msun component masses, 60-200 Msun total, anti-aligned spins up to 0.99, reduced to 55 bases over 2 time slices, only the final slice (37 bases) used. LVK-consistent bank: 53 templates, 20-40 Msun, non-spinning, 50 bases over 2 slices (30 used).
models.data: Simulated only. One month of stationary Gaussian noise coloured to aLIGO design sensitivity (data reused from the authors' ref. [92]). 1e4 signals per class injected with SNR uniform in [8,100] (not volume-distributed): glitch-like BBHs (uniform 10-100 Msun, spins |s_z|<0.99), LVK-consistent BBHs (20-40 Msun, non-spinning); 1e4 blip glitches from gengli (GAN, 30-250 Hz), 1e4 scattering-light arches (3 arches, f_mod U(0.05,0.3) Hz, f_harm,0 U(16,20) Hz, spacing U(3,10) Hz, SNR 8-100) and a Gaussian-noise class. Templates for SVD from SEOBNRv4_ROM; no real LIGO strain or Gravity Spy data is used (gengli was trained on Gravity Spy blips).
models.training: 80/10/10 train/validation/test split, equal glitch and signal counts; weighted binary cross-entropy with weight 10 on noise-transient samples and 1 on signals (to mimic the glitch:signal rate imbalance, blips ~100/day vs a candidate GW every ~2 days); Adam. Learning rate, batch size and epochs not stated. Decision threshold fixed at 0.5 because outputs are saturated near 0/1.
models.results: Row-normalised confusion matrices for 24 classifiers (Figs 3-4): TPR 0.941-0.999 and FPR 0.000-0.004 (0.001-0.004 for blips). Toy ranking-statistic pipeline at rho_bar=7: TPR 92-94%, FPR 0.25-1% (inconsistent in text); at rho_bar=10 TPR 84%, FPR <~0.1%. With the p_glitch weight TPR rises 94->98% (rho_bar 7) and 84->90% (rho_bar 10), FPR falls to <~0.1%. No sensitive-volume, FAR (per year) or real-data result; proof of concept only.
models.code: No code link in the paper (GitHub search for the title/first author found nothing definitive; see code_repos).
models.gaps: Simulated stationary Gaussian noise only; blips/arches are model glitches (gengli, analytic arches), not real Gravity Spy transients; single detector only (coincidence ignored, acknowledged); toy pipeline rather than the real GstLAL rank statistic; no FAR per unit time or sensitive volume; training hyperparameters unstated; FPR resolution limited to ~0.1% by ~1000 test samples while real search backgrounds need ~1e-6 or lower.
models.adaptation_notes: CNN on basis-response images for signal consistency.

models.comparability_notes_extractor: Classification of simulated glitches vs simulated BBH responses on balanced test sets at p=0.5; not comparable to detection TPR at a FAR per year or to Gravity Spy accuracy. Compare only as a signal-consistency veto (TPR/FPR at fixed threshold) against another veto on the same simulated sets.
suspected_errors_extracted: The Fig. 3 caption gives the top-left classifier a 99% true positive rate and 0.7% false positive rate. In the printed matrix the Positive row has 0.993 (TPR) and FNR 0.007, and the Negative row has FPR 0.003, so the quoted 0.7% is the false-negative rate, not the FPR.

Toy-pipeline numbers at rho_bar=7 disagree within the paper: text Sec. III C says 92% TPR / 0.25% FPR; Fig. 7 caption says 94% TPR and FPRs of 0.7% (low) and <~0.1% (high); the weighted-pipeline paragraph says TPR rises 'from 94%' and FPR drops 'from 1%'. Three different FPRs (0.25%, 0.7%, 1%) for the same threshold.
Abstract headline 'accurately classifies >~99%' is stronger than the matrices (0.941-0.995 TPR); the all-glitches+noise classifiers reach only 0.941-0.994.
Recall defined as 'fraction of positive predictions out of all positives' (should be true positives out of all positives); minor wording error.

models.title: Classification uncertainty for transient gravitational-wave noise artefacts with optimised conformal prediction
models.authors: Ann-Kristin Malz, Gregory Ashton, Nicolo Colombo
models.access: Open arXiv; full PDF read (text extracted page by page; key figures and tables viewed as images).
models.architecture: No new neural network. Conformal prediction (split, Mondrian/label-conditional) is wrapped around the pre-trained Gravity Spy CNN classifier's 22-class softmax scores. Eight parameterised nonconformity measures A(x,y) are compared (baseline 1-f_y, softmax, entropy, entropy-softmax, margin2, maxscore2, CNN, Brier; Table I) and their parameters optimised (grid search then L-BFGS-B) for F1 score, singleton count, or average prediction-set size. Output is a prediction set Gamma_alpha of glitch labels with guaranteed (1-alpha) marginal and per-class coverage.
models.inputs: Gravity Spy classifier output scores f_y(x) (22 classes) and the dataset's true label; CP itself never sees images, strain or time series.
models.data: Gravity Spy 'retired' dataset (Zenodo records for O1, O2, O3a, O3b; each glitch has ML scores and a combined volunteer+ML final_label). Highly unbalanced (327,262 Scattered Light; 1,167 Wandering Line), so up to 1500 glitches per class are sampled. Split 50/50 into optimisation and evaluation sets, each 50/50 into calibration and test; five optimisation repeats with different splits.
models.training: No training of the CNN. CP calibration computes per-class quantile q_y=s_ceil((N_y+1)(1-alpha)) of nonconformity scores on the calibration set. Nonconformity-measure parameters are optimised (grid + L-BFGS-B, regularisation rho=1e-5*(params squared) to remove degeneracy for entropy measures) at alpha=0.1.
models.results: At alpha=0.1 the baseline 1-f_y measure gives macro F1 0.456, singleton fraction 0.179 and mean set size 4.263 of 22 labels; optimisation never beats the baseline on F1 or set size (parameters collapse to baseline), while every optimised measure raises the singleton fraction to 0.237-0.271 (maxscore2 best). Multi-class ROC AUC 0.929 (CP) vs 0.861 (Gravity Spy raw). Tomte needs 1-alpha~0.5 and Scattered Light ~0.9 for singleton sets on average.
models.code: Example code archived on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.14066270, ref. [30]); no GitHub link in the paper.
models.gaps: Not a detection or noise-rejection result; 'true' labels are not ground truth (ML-contaminated); outdated Gravity Spy model; no real-time or per-detector evaluation; figures 5, 9, 11 not value-read (Table II and text values extracted instead); only alpha=0.1 tabulated.
models.adaptation_notes: Conformal prediction on Gravity Spy scores.

models.comparability_notes_extractor: Uncertainty quantification on top of the Gravity Spy classifier; macro-F1/set-size are set-valued metrics and are NOT comparable to single-label glitch-classification accuracy or F1 in other papers. Calibration data are Gravity Spy final_label, not independent ground truth.
suspected_errors_extracted: Table II extraction is ragged: 'Softmax' and 'Entropy' rows are merged on one line and 'CNN' and 'Brier' share the parameter block; the parsing of which score belongs to which measure is by row order and was matched to Fig. 9, not independently verified.
The text says the Fig. 4 plot is truncated at 1-alpha=0.9 because the set size reaches the total glitch count (22); but 22 is the number of classes (labels), not of glitches (a wording slip).

Reported Gravity Spy accuracy on this dataset is stated by the authors to be 'significantly' lower than the published Gravity Spy accuracy because the 'true label' (final_label) is partly the ML label itself and the ML model has since been improved; macro-F1 0.456 is therefore not an estimate of Gravity Spy's true accuracy, and the CNN scores come from an older Gravity Spy model.
Singleton metric is called 'average number of singletons' in the text but Eq. 6 normalises by N, so it is a fraction; Table II values 0.18-0.27 are therefore fractions, not counts.

models.title: Evaluating Deep Learning Models for Multiclass Classification of LIGO Gravitational-Wave Glitches
models.authors: Rudhresh Manoharan, Gerald Cleaver
models.venue: arXiv preprint (no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv; full PDF read (text extracted page by page; key figures and tables viewed as images).
models.architecture: Benchmark of ten tabular models, not a new architecture: XGBoost (gradient-boosted trees), MLP, TabNet, TabTransformer, FT-Transformer, AutoInt, DANet, NODE, GATE and GANDALF via PyTorch Tabular (PyTorch Lightning); Optuna search of 100 trials per model with stratified 3-fold CV on the training set. Interpretability with Captum (neural) and TreeSHAP (XGBoost), compared by Spearman rank correlation.
models.inputs: Nine numeric per-glitch features from the Gravity Spy O3 metadata (Table I): peak_time, peak_time_ns, start_time_ns, duration, peak_frequency, central_freq, amplitude, snr, q_value. No images, no strain.
models.data: Gravity Spy O3 dataset (Zenodo 5649212): ~5e5 labelled glitches, 24 classes (including No_Glitch and None_of_the_Above), severely imbalanced (log-scale histogram, Scattered_Light largest). Two stratified datasets: sampled 5e4 and full ~5e5; 64/16/20 train/val/test.
models.training: Weighted F1 selection metric; best of 100 Optuna trials by 3-fold CV weighted F1; early stopping on validation; final model retrained with 15 random seeds and mean test weighted F1 reported; best validation checkpoint. Hardware: Baylor Kodiak HPC (details not given).
models.results: No numeric table: results are in scatter and box figures. Read from Fig. 4/5: XGBoost ~0.853 weighted F1 (best, fits in ~35 s), MLP ~0.825, TabNet ~0.80, FT-Transformer ~0.79, AutoInt ~0.79, GANDALF/DANet ~0.775, GATE ~0.765, NODE ~0.74, TabTransformer ~0.68. Feature-importance alignment with XGBoost highest for NODE (rho 0.72) and MLP (0.66), negative for TabNet and DANet. Text names DANet 'best model' for the confusion matrix (contradiction).
models.code: Authors' GitHub repository github.com/rudhresh1997/glitch-tabular-prd and Zenodo release doi 10.5281/zenodo.19475319; dataset Zenodo 5649212.
models.gaps: No numeric table of final F1 (read from figures only); dataset identity of Fig. 3/4/5 unclear; Fig. 5 units implausible; timestamp features possibly leak class; no per-class precision/recall values; no comparison to image-based Gravity Spy CNN on the same split.
models.adaptation_notes: Tabular deep models on Gravity Spy O3 metadata.

comparability.what_differs: Tabular metadata including timestamps.
highlighted_errors: Discussion calls DANet the best model while XGBoost leads Figs 3-4.
Fig 3 box-plot medians (0.11-0.43) are inconsistent with Figs 4-6 (0.68-0.85).
Per-sample inference times of seconds to minutes on 9 features are not credible.

models.comparability_notes_extractor: Tabular-metadata glitch classification on 9 features, weighted F1 on a 24-class imbalanced split; not comparable to image-based Gravity Spy accuracy/F1 (different inputs, class set including No_Glitch/None_of_the_Above) and weighted F1 is dominated by Scattered_Light/Fast_Scattering support.
suspected_errors_extracted: Text calls XGBoost the best on median F1 (Fig. 3, Fig. 4: ~0.85 vs MLP ~0.83) but Sec. IV G and the Discussion call DANet 'the best-performing model' and show its confusion matrix; DANet is ~0.775 on Fig. 4, fifth-ninth place.

Fig. 3 box plots (medians 0.11 TabTransformer, 0.17 NODE, 0.43 GATE; boxes spanning ~0.0-0.85) are wildly inconsistent with the Fig. 4/5/6 mean weighted F1 values (0.68-0.85) and with the claim XGBoost has a 'relatively narrow interquartile range' (its box spans ~0.47-0.85); the Fig. 3 sample must include failed Optuna trials or both datasets, but this is not stated.

Fig. 5 is captioned 'per-sample inference time' in seconds, with values 0.15 s (TabTransformer) to ~300 s (NODE) and 0.2 s for XGBoost on 9 features; per-sample times of seconds are not credible and cannot be reconciled with the text's 'millisecond scale' target. The axis is probably the total time for N=10112 samples (so ~20 us/sample for XGBoost) or mislabelled.
Fig. 6 shows XGBoost at weighted F1 ~0.862 whereas Figs 4 and 5 show ~0.853 while all other models coincide; reading-level discrepancy (~0.009) that may mean Fig. 6 is the full dataset only.

Features include peak_time, peak_time_ns and start_time_ns (GPS timestamps). Timestamps correlate with glitch class through run epoch and detector state, so they can leak class information that is not morphological; no ablation is reported. Also the 'tabular' 9 features are not what Gravity Spy classifies from (images), so F1 ~0.85 is not comparable to Gravity Spy's image accuracy.

models.title: Improving early detection of gravitational waves from binary neutron stars using CNNs and FPGAs
models.authors: Ana Martins, Melissa Lopez, Quirijn Meijer, Gregory Baltus, Marc van der Sluys, Chris Van Den Broeck et al.
models.venue: arXiv preprint (no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv; full PDF read (text extracted page by page; key figures and tables viewed as images).
models.architecture: GWaveNet: 7 WaveNet gated residual modules (causal dilated Conv1D, kernel 16, 64 filters, dilation 2^i for i=0..6, batch norm, tanh x sigmoid gating, skip sums), then 1x1 conv and two dense layers (2496->50->1), BCE-with-logits; 522,598 trainable parameters, 3 detector channels in one model. Baseline FindCNN (Baltus et al.): batchnorm + 5 conv blocks (kernels 16,8,4,8,16; filters 32,64,128,256,256; stride 4) + 2 dense layers, 6,179,303 parameters. 2D and FPGA-modified variants (FindCNN2D, FindCNN2DModified, GWaveNet2D, GWaveNet2DModified; GWaveNet kernels cut to 2, 32 filters, linearised activations) made to fit the AMD Kria KV260 DPU with Vitis AI power-of-two quantization; no GWaveNet variant could be compiled for the FPGA.
models.inputs: 300 s of whitened (10-100 Hz band-pass), [-1,1]-normalised strain at 512 Hz (155,648 samples) from H1, L1 and V1 as three channels; partial inspiral only (earlier signals have lower fmax).
models.data: Simulated: Gaussian noise coloured with PyCBC O3 average PSDs (aLIGO140MpcT1800545, aLIGOAdVO3LowT1800545); BNS m1,m2 U[1,3] Msun, SpinTaylorT4 inspiral, random sky and spins; balanced noise vs noise+signal. Five curriculum datasets D1-D5 with average fmax 40,35,30,25,20 Hz, each 22,600 samples; per step 71/9/20 train/val/test on cumulative union of datasets.
models.training: Progressive curriculum learning (descending fmax), cumulative data. FindCNN: 6 epochs/step, weighted BCEWithLogits (positive weight 0.4), AdaMax lr 8e-5, wd 1e-5. GWaveNet: early stopping (eps 1e-4, patience 2) per step, positive-class weight 0.1, AdamW lr0=2e-5 divided by curriculum step. PyTorch; V100 for training, GTX 1080 for testing/energy.
models.results: Test TPR ('accuracy') at FAP=1%: GWaveNet 76.22% vs FindCNN 66.81%; 2D versions 79.42% and 69.50%; FPGA-compatible FindCNN2DModified 66.70% (65.07% quantized). GWaveNet FAP=1% at threshold 0.46 (FindCNN 0.86) and reaches FAP<=1e-4. GWaveNet avoids catastrophic forgetting seen in FindCNN (about -20 pp on easier fmax 35-40 Hz sets). Inference per 300 s sample: FindCNN ~22-30 ms CPU/GPU, 84 ms on FPGA; GWaveNet 155 ms CPU, 34 ms GPU. Energy 0.1-1 J/sample; FPGA ~7x cheapest including hardware cost.
models.code: github.com/anaismartins/deploying-custom-nn-in-fpga (footnote in paper); see code_repos.
models.gaps: Simulated Gaussian noise only (no real O3 data, no glitches); FAP=1% per sample is far from realistic FARs; balanced set; no PE or sky localisation; GWaveNet not deployed on FPGA; no multi-seed variance on accuracies (Table 2 has no error bars); no sensitive distance or FAR/year.
models.adaptation_notes: GWaveNet on 300 s three-detector windows; FPGA quantisation.
models.effort_basis: rule from the tags' one-off efforts (any L or >= 3 M: L; any M or >= 4 S: M; else S; unread: -)

suspected_errors_extracted: Sec. 6 says 'FindCNN is ~2 ms faster on GPU', but Table 3 gives 21.75 ms (FindCNN) vs 33.60 ms (GWaveNet), a difference of ~12 ms (the text elsewhere says 1.5x, consistent with the table).
Table 1 lists five curriculum datasets but only four PISNR values (34.5, 34.7, 34.7, 34.6), so one value is missing from the extracted table; the mapping to D1-D5 is ambiguous.

Table 2 is extracted column-major with garbled blanks; the row assignment used here (FindCNN2D 69.50/69.37, FindCNN2DModified 66.70/65.07, GWaveNet2D 79.42/77.28, GWaveNet2DModified 71.72/72.42) was inferred to satisfy every comparison in the text (2D ~3 pp above 1D, modified ~5 pp below GWaveNet, GWaveNet2DModified +~1 pp after quantization, worst GWaveNet ~2 pp above best FindCNN), not read directly.

FindCNN is called 'GregNet' in the legends of Fig. 6 (and apparently Fig. 5), whereas the text calls it FindCNN; the catalogue's previous entry attributed FindCNN as this paper's model, but FindCNN is the Baltus et al. baseline (ref. [29]) and the paper's own model is GWaveNet.

'Accuracy at FAP=1%' is a TPR at a per-sample false alarm probability of 1% on a balanced dataset; 1% per 300 s segment is orders of magnitude above any realistic search FAR, so the headline 76.22% vs 66.81% is not a detection-pipeline sensitivity.

Test-sample counts: 22,000 for most models but only 5,000 for post-quantization GWaveNet2D/GWaveNet2DModified; their quantization-induced changes (-2.1 pp and +0.7 pp) are within roughly 1.3 pp binomial error at 5000 samples.
Table 3 energy of FindCNN on CPU (107 mJ) vs FindCNN2D (178 mJ) differ by 66% for the same ~28 ms time, which looks like a measurement/variant artefact rather than a real difference.

models.title: Deep learning merger masses estimation from gravitational waves signals in the frequency domain
models.authors: Juan Pablo Marulanda, Camilo Santa, Antonio Enea Romano
models.venue: arXiv preprint (no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv; full PDF read (text extracted page by page; key figures and tables viewed as images).
models.architecture: FCNN: 2D CNN on a zero-padded spectrogram image (32x127x1): three conv layers (16, 8, 4 filters, ReLU) -> pooling -> flatten 1024 -> dense 32 -> 16 -> 2 outputs (m1, m2); ~50,000 parameters (Table II). Benchmark TCNN (from Gabbard-style ref. [7], Table I): 1D conv 16/32/64 filters with pooling on the 8192-sample time series -> dense 64 -> 2; ~550,000 parameters. Regression of the two component masses, MAPE loss.
models.inputs: Spectrogram (dB, eq. 3) of 1 s of strain at 4096 Hz (windows of 128, zero-padding 896, overlap 64), cropped to <=120 Hz, min-max normalised; TCNN takes the raw 8192-sample series.
models.data: Simulated only: PyCBC SEOBNRv4 BBH, zero spin and eccentricity, m1,m2 10-75 Msun (q<10), fixed distance 2000 Mpc, two datasets with polarization 0 and pi/2; random time shift in [0,0.2] s; coloured noise from aLIGOZeroDetHighPower PSD at SNR 5-25; 9346 mergers split 50/50 modelling/validation on an interleaved mass grid, modelling 70/30 train/development.
models.training: 1000 epochs on 4673 signals, minimising MAPE of both masses; development set used to choose architecture; optimiser and learning rate not stated.
models.results: MAPE falls from ~80-90% at SNR 5 to ~5-7% at SNR 25 for both networks; FCNN slightly better below SNR~12 and ~equal above. Over-fit estimator ~0.8-0.9 for TCNN versus ~0.1-0.3 for FCNN above SNR 10. FCNN pipeline including spectrogram only ~6% slower than TCNN.

models.gaps: Simulated noise only (no real data, no glitches); only masses estimated, no uncertainty or posterior; no matched-filter or Bayesian comparison; fixed distance, fixed sky/orientation, zero spin; interleaved train/validation grid; only baseline is a reproduced TCNN; Figs 8-10 not value-read; hardware and optimiser unstated.

models.comparability_notes_extractor: Point-estimate regression of component masses on simulated aLIGO-PSD noise, reported as MAPE vs SNR; not comparable to posterior-based PE metrics (p-p, KL, coverage) or to detection metrics. Compare only against Gabbard-style TCNN regression with identical SNR definition.
suspected_errors_extracted: Text states masses 10-75 Msun, but the Fig. 5 mass-pair scatter extends down to ~5 Msun in m2 (lower edge near m2~5-8) and the example in Fig. 1 is 57+33 Msun; the stated range is inconsistent with the plotted grid.

Distance fixed at 2000 Mpc yet SNRs span 5-25; how SNR was varied (rescaling the noise or the amplitude?) is not stated, and the abstract's claim that FCNN has a 'slightly better' MAPE is within the point-to-point scatter of Fig. 6 above SNR~12.

Modelling and validation sets are interleaved on the same mass grid (Fig. 5), so 'validation' tests interpolation between neighbouring training masses, not generalisation; MAPE and the over-fit estimator are optimistic. Eq. 5 defines over-fit with 'test error' while the text uses validation error.

Over-fit estimator for TCNN stays ~0.8-0.9 at every SNR (training error ~10x lower than validation error) while Fig. 6 shows MAPE >20% at SNR<10; this shows the benchmark TCNN is badly over-parametrised, so the FCNN comparison is against a weak baseline reproduced from ref. [7].
MAPE is defined (eq. 6) without a factor 100 and with an index over both masses; units are not stated and the quoted MAPE >80 at SNR 5 implies percent.

models.title: A machine learning-enabled search for binary black hole mergers in LIGO-Virgo-KAGRAs third observing run
models.authors: Ethan Marx, William Benoit, Trevor Blodgett, Deep Chatterjee, Emma de Bruin, Steven Henderson et al.
models.venue: arXiv preprint (no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv; full PDF read (text extracted page by page; key figures and tables viewed as images).
models.architecture: Aframe (ML4GW): supervised ResNet34-style 1D CNN producing a scalar detection statistic from overlapping 1.5 s windows (stride 0.25 s, 4 Hz inference) of coincident H1+L1 strain; output integrated by a top-hat filter and peaks identified as candidates; FAR from timeslides; p_astro from a foreground/background model (Appendix A) using only the detection statistic. Trained on 8x NVIDIA A100 with learning rate scaled linearly by GPU count.
models.inputs: Whitened (via per-segment PSD, segments >=128 s), 2048 Hz, high-passed at 32 Hz strain from H1 and L1 (coincident only; Virgo not used); CAT1/CAT2 veto flags applied.
models.data: Training: simulated BBH waveforms injected in real O3 strain, first 17 days of O3 (2019-04-01 to 04-17), component masses 5-100 Msun (m^-2.35 primary), redshift 0-2 comoving, isotropic spins up to 0.998. Analysis: all public O3 H1/L1 data with science flag (202.4 d live time). Background: 100 yr from timeslides; foreground: injection campaign across O3 excluding training period.
models.training: Per the Aframe recipe of Marx et al. PRD 111, 042010 (ref. [15]); scaled to 8 A100s; details not repeated here.
models.results: Sensitive volume vs FAR (Fig. 2) read for four log-normal mass distributions; Aframe is competitive or better at high masses (35+35 Msun: ~16 Gpc^3 at 100/yr vs GstLAL ~12) but 30-50% below matched filtering at 20+10 Msun. Search finds 41 significant (p_astro>0.5) candidates, 38 of 70 H1/L1 GWTC-3 events (27 at p_astro>0.99), plus 2 IAS and 1 OGC events; no new candidates (a p_astro=0.6 event is vetoed due to a whistle glitch). Compared with GstLAL 47, MBTA 48 etc.
models.code: Aframe code at github.com/ML4GW/aframe (ref. [16]); see code_repos.
models.gaps: H1/L1 only (loses Virgo-dependent events); training prior m2>=5 Msun (misses GW190814 etc.); p_astro model ignores source properties; sensitivity lower at low chirp mass; per-event table values not verified; single trained model, no seeds variance.

models.title: Using machine learning to auto-tune chi-squared tests for gravitational wave searches
models.authors: Connor McIsaac, Ian Harry
models.access: Open arXiv; full PDF read (text extracted page by page; key figures and tables viewed as images).
models.architecture: Learned signal-consistency (chi^2) test for the PyCBC matched-filter search, not a classifier. A dense net maps each search template to a time shift and a frequency shift (4 nets with 11 dense layers each, first 6 layers shared; input 2440 samples = |template| sampled 12-256 Hz at 0.1 Hz; widths 128,128,64,64,32,32,16,16,8,8, tanh output scaled by dt_max, df_max); the shifted template is orthogonalised against the search template to give 4 chi^2 templates. A learned 4-parameter re-weighting (sigma, alpha, beta, delta; eq. 12) converts chi^2_r into a re-weighted SNR. Matched filter and chi^2 are implemented in TensorFlow and trained end to end with stochastic gradient descent.
models.inputs: 64 s of 2048 Hz strain (12 Hz high-pass, PSD from 512 s) around a trigger and its search template (SEOBNRv4_ROM); triggers carry rho, rho_sg.
models.data: Real O3 (first half) PyCBC IMBH search data, 45 days: single-detector noise triggers with rho_sg>6, 6<=rho<=64, coincident ones removed, clustered over 1 s; plus recovered simulated signals (FAR<1/yr, same cuts; NRSur7DQ4, SEOBNRv4, SEOBNRv4HM, so including precession and higher modes). 1200 noise and 1200 signal samples per SNR bin (bins 6,8,10,14,18,24,64) = 14,400; 90/10 train/validation = 12,960/1,440.
models.training: Batches of 32; noise loss max(rho_hat-4,0), signal loss rho-rho_hat; Nesterov-momentum SGD; pre-train re-weighting parameters then train everything; 25 passes over the training set (~24 h, 8 CPU cores); learning rate x0.9 per pass.
models.results: Held-out 8 d IMBH search: new tuned chi^2 test reduces single-detector triggers in H1, L1 and V1 and raises sensitive volume-time at FAR 1/yr by ~4% for M_tot 100-300 Msun and ~11% for 300-600 Msun (bands from +2% to +17%, Fig. 5). Signals are largely unaffected (SNR removal small) while noise triggers have ~half their SNR removed.
models.code: No code link; trained parameters provided at https://icg-gravwaves.github.io/chisqnet/ (supplementary data file); see code_repos.
models.gaps: One search configuration (IMBH) and one 8-day test stretch; no uncertainty on volume ratios; no per-event result; the framework is described as general but only one model is trained; code not released beyond parameters.
models.adaptation_notes: Learned chi-squared tuning inside the PyCBC IMBH search.
models.effort_basis: rule from the tags' one-off efforts (any L or >= 3 M: L; any M or >= 4 S: M; else S; unread: -)

models.comparability_notes_extractor: Relative sensitive-volume-time gain of a modified PyCBC IMBH search at FAR 1/yr; comparable only to other re-rankings of the same search/data stretch; not comparable to standalone neural-network detection metrics or to absolute sensitive volumes.
suspected_errors_extracted: Abstract/text say '~11% for signals with masses >300 Msun' while Fig. 5 shows +17% in the highest-mass band and non-monotonic bands (+2, +5, +11, +8, +17% ordered by increasing mass); the 11% is an unspecified average, and no uncertainty is given from the 8-day test stretch (few injections per band).
Fig. 5 colourbar spans 1.04-1.16 yet the lowest band is labelled +2% (ratio 1.02, below the colourbar floor).

Training noise triggers are selected with rho_sg>6 and 6<=rho<=64 and coincident triggers removed; the held-out 8 d test uses single-detector triggers in the same way, so the improvement partly reflects the training-selection distribution; no real-event (GW190521-like) check is reported.

models.title: Rapid Mass Parameter Estimation of Binary Black Hole Coalescences Using Deep Learning
models.authors: Alistair McLeod, Daniel Jacobs, Chayan Chatterjee, Linqing Wen, Fiona Panther
models.venue: arXiv preprint (no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv; full PDF read (text extracted page by page; key figures and tables viewed as images).
models.architecture: Two separate CNN estimators (chirp mass, mass ratio) fed by a denoising autoencoder (Chatterjee et al.). Estimator: two input branches (H1, L1), each with 1D convolutions and residual blocks (x3 repeated), concatenated into dense layers with dropout (256 neurons per layer for chirp mass, 64 for mass ratio), then a TensorFlow Probability IndependentNormal layer giving a mean and standard deviation; trained with negative log-likelihood and Adam (Keras/TensorFlow). Component masses by solving Mc and q for m1,m2 with 10,000 posterior samples.
models.inputs: Denoised H1 and L1 0.25 s time series at 2048 Hz (autoencoder output).
models.data: 500,000 simulated BBH (SEOBNRv4), parameters in Table I (Mc 6-70 Msun, q 0.1-1, m1,m2 7-100 Msun, d 40-3000 Mpc, SNR 10-30, spin -1..0.99), Gaussian noise coloured by O2 PSD, uniform in the target parameter per network; test on 25,000 unseen simulated signals plus the 10 O1/O2 BBH events from GWOSC.

models.title: Gravitational-Wave Searches for Cosmic String Cusps in Einstein Telescope Data using Deep Learning
models.authors: Quirijn Meijer, Melissa Lopez, Daichi Tsuna, Sarah Caudill
models.venue: arXiv preprint (no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv; full PDF read (text extracted page by page; key figures and tables viewed as images).
models.architecture: Ensemble of three binary WaveNet-style CNNs, one per Einstein Telescope stream, with probabilities averaged P=(P0+P1+P2)/3 (no coincidence input). Each network: 11 dilated Conv1D modules (kernel 3, dilation 2^k) with tanh x sigmoid gating, 1x1 convolutions, residual and skip connections, then dense layers (57,348 -> 50 -> 2, softmax); non-causal, no 256-level amplitude quantisation. PyTorch. Interpretability: waveform 'surgery' (excising peak/downtaper/tail sections), 1D activation visualisation, PCA of the penultimate dense layer.
models.inputs: Whitened ET strain time series, 3 streams x 8 s at 8192 Hz (65,536 samples per stream), no further preprocessing.
models.data: Simulated: ET design-sensitivity PSD (PyCBC) Gaussian noise, cusp waveform h(f)=A f^(-4/3)(f_high-f)_+ (LALSimulation, A U[1e-23,1e-21] Hz^(1/3), f_high U{20..4000} Hz) vs blip glitches from gengli (GAN trained on O2 LIGO blips; ~10% outliers rejected) scaled to cusp SNR distribution; 30,000 examples (16,000/4,000/10,000 train/val/test), balanced.
models.training: AdamW lr 1e-4, wd 1e-3, batch 13 (memory-limited), 20 epochs per network with epochs of best validation loss chosen per stream; thresholds 0.4-0.6 scanned on validation (0.5 kept); V100 GPU.
models.results: Test set (10,000): accuracy 78.76%, TPR 75.52%, FPR 18.00% (TP 37.8%, FP 9.0%, FN 12.2%, TN 41.0%); ~10 ms per 3x8 s example. On a 400-sample comparison set the ROC of the model is far above matched filtering with 20 random cusp templates, which falls below the diagonal. Surgery: removal of the glitch peak changes the ensemble probability by 0.16 on average (max 0.83); tails and downtapers matter little.
models.code: No code link found in the paper or by a title search (see code_repos).
models.gaps: Simulated ET noise only (Gaussian), glitches are GAN-modelled LIGO blips, not ET glitches; no real data; no coincidence or sky localisation; no FAR/efficiency vs SNR curve; matched-filter baseline weak and ROC below random (suspect); single dataset split, no seeds variance.
models.adaptation_notes: ET three-stream cusp-vs-blip classifier; needs the ET response and a cusp generator.

models.comparability_notes_extractor: Binary cusp-vs-blip classification on a balanced simulated ET set with matched SNR distributions (accuracy 78.8%, TPR 75.5% at FPR 18%); not comparable to efficiency at FAR/yr or to LIGO-data burst searches; compare only to classifiers using the same gengli+cusp ET dataset.
suspected_errors_extracted: Sec. V B concludes matched filtering is 'worse than random' on the signal-vs-glitch task (ROC below the diagonal). For signals matched against the exact injected waveform (the optimum filter) this should give AUC>0.5 unless glitch amplitudes scaled to 'follow the same SNR distribution' give glitches a systematically higher maximum SNR; an AUC<0.5 indicates a possible bug or SNR-definition mismatch between the cusp injection and the whitened gengli injection, not a property of matched filtering.

The matched-filter comparison uses only 400 examples and a template bank of 20 random cusp signals whose choice is described as 'arbitrary'; the authors call this conservative, but results cannot be generalised to a real search.

Training/validation/ test glitches are injected with uncorrelated offsets per stream (no coincidence), and cusp signals are injected coherently via the ET antenna pattern; the network may learn cross-stream coherence of the injection, not morphology, although the ensemble design is meant to block this.

Overfitting starts after 2-4 epochs and the chosen epochs [2,4,2] were fine-tuned by brute-force over the ensemble lattice and thresholds on the validation set (an optimistic selection), but the final metrics are on the separate test set, so the effect is limited.

models.title: Robustness of Deep Learning Models to Precession in Gravitational-Wave Searches for Intermediate-Mass Black Hole Binaries
models.authors: Quirijn Meijer, Marc van der Sluys, Sarah Caudill
models.venue: arXiv preprint (no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv; full PDF read (text extracted page by page; key figures and tables viewed as images).
models.architecture: WaveNet-style 1D CNN binary classifier (same architecture as Meijer et al. cosmic-string work, dense layer resized for 4096 Hz input): gated dilated convolutions with tanh x sigmoid, residual and skip connections, dense layers, 2-way softmax; PyTorch on an NVIDIA A30. Three classifiers: A (aligned-spin only), P (precessing only), C (curriculum: first trained on aligned-spin data then continued on precessing data, 'transfer + curriculum learning'). Interpretation: PCA, t-SNE, Pearson/Spearman correlations of outputs with waveform parameters (chi_p, total mass, mass ratio, inclination), false-negative analysis.
models.inputs: 4 s whitened single-detector (H1) strain at 4096 Hz (16,384 samples); no spectrogram.
models.data: Simulated: IMRPhenomTP IMBH waveforms (aligned or precessing), M_tot 150-600 Msun, q 1-10, spins up to 0.99, d log-uniform 200-220 Mpc, injected into Gaussian noise coloured by the O3 Hanford PSD (first 3 months); 50,000 blip glitches from gengli (GAN on O2 blips; similarity metrics Wasserstein, match, cross-covariance); signal and glitch SNR distributions made identical (Fig. 1). Datasets A+G and P+G of 100,000 each (shared glitches), 70k/10k/20k.
models.training: AdamW lr 1e-4, wd 1e-3, batch 30, 20 epochs with overfitting after ~5 epochs; stopping epoch 5 for A and P; curriculum: A+G trained to epoch 2/5/7 then P+G continued, best [5,2]; threshold 0.5; cross-entropy loss.
models.results: On balanced 20,000-sample test sets: aligned classifier accuracy 0.9498 (A+G) and 0.9474 (P+G); precessing 0.9410 and 0.9388; curriculum 0.9547 and 0.9509 (TPR 0.9332/0.9254, FPR 0.0238/0.0237); AUC 0.9486 / 0.9399 / 0.9527. All strongly outperform matched filtering on this task; classifier mistakes correlate most strongly with chi_p/precession rather than total mass; precession-trained classifier has more false positives on glitches.
models.code: No code link found in the paper or by a title search (see code_repos).
models.gaps: Simulated Gaussian noise (one PSD) and GAN-modelled blip glitches only; single detector; no real O3 data; no FAR or sensitive-volume result; matched-filter baseline is deliberately weak (20 templates; exact template for signals); single training run per classifier.

models.comparability_notes_extractor: Accuracy/TPR/FPR on a balanced simulated signal-vs-blip set with matched SNR distributions (no FAR); comparable only to the same gengli+IMRPhenomTP dataset and to Meijer et al. 2023; not comparable to sensitive volume or efficiency at FAR/yr.
suspected_errors_extracted: Sec. V A says that when two classifiers perform equally, 'the classifier with the lowest true positive rate will be favoured' because a pipeline would rather veto false positives; but the curriculum classifier is then chosen as the one with the highest TPR ([5,2]). The first rule should refer to the lowest FPR; the selection rule is stated inconsistently.

C[A+G] has TN=9762, FP=238 and C[P+G] TN=9763, FP=237 although both test sets share the same 10,000 glitches and the classifier is the same; a one-count difference is unexplained (non-deterministic inference or a counting slip). A and P classifiers have identical glitch counts across both sets.

Curriculum classifier has the highest accuracy and TPR but also the highest FPR (2.4% vs 1.5% for A); accuracy differences of 0.5-1.6 percentage points between classifiers are based on a single training run with epochs/stopping times chosen on validation (three curriculum candidates tried), without seed variance, so the ranking is uncertain.

Distance is fixed to 200-220 Mpc and the SNR distributions of signals and glitches are forced to coincide (Fig. 1, 0-200); accuracy is then a classification result at matched SNR with no FAR; a 95% accuracy at 1.5-2.4% FPR is far from the 1e-5-1e-8 per-segment rates needed in a search.

Total Model Loss averages MAEs of quantities with different units (Msun, Mpc, degrees, dimensionless); I verified it equals the mean of the six MAEs (hybrid DeepModel 55.1748/6 = 9.1958), so it is dominated by distance and carries no physical meaning.
Dataset arithmetic: 70% of 5,820,000 = 4,074,000; 90%/10% gives 3,666,600 train and 407,400 validation, but text says 407,000 validation (minor typo).

Parameters come from a coarse discrete grid (integer masses, distance steps of 50 Mpc, 5 inclinations, spins in steps of 0.5) and train/val/test are a random split of that grid, so the test set is almost entirely interpolation within seen parameter combinations; only the noise realisation differs. Quoted MAEs are optimistic for continuous priors.

Min-max normalisation of each strain to [0,1] removes absolute amplitude, so distance can only be inferred from relative signal-to-noise structure; the noise PSD, injection SNR and noise realisation scheme are not stated.

Real-event event name "GW191216_21338" is truncated (GW191216_213338); the bound-based MAE criterion assigns zero error inside catalogue intervals, which makes real-event numbers incomparable with the simulated-data MAE. n=5 events, authors acknowledge.

models.title: Comparative study of 1D and 2D convolutional neural network models with attribution analysis for gravitational wave detection from compact binary coalescences
models.authors: Seiya Sasaoka, Naoki Koyama, Diego Dominguez, Yusuke Sakai, Kentaro Somiya, Yuto Omae et al.

models.architecture: 1D CNN: ResNet-54 with deep adaptive input normalisation (Nousi et al.), 3-channel (H1,L1,V1) whitened series, 1,935,698 parameters. 2D CNN: ResNet-50 on 3-channel Q-transform maps, 23,508,548 parameters. Ensemble: FC head (10240 -> 200 -> 4, LeakyReLU, dropout 0.25) on concatenated 1D+2D features; final output = 0.4*1D + 0.4*2D + 0.2*head. Four-class output (BBH, NSBH, BNS, noise). t-SNE and integrated-gradients attribution analysis.

models.data: Non-precessing signals: BBH SEOBNRv4 (5-80 Msun), NSBH and BNS SpinTaylorT4 (NS 1-2 Msun, BH 5-35 Msun), aligned spins 0-0.99, injected in real O3 noise from GWOSC (train GPS 1238163456-1238659072, val 1238663168-1239162880, test 1239166976-1239875584; GWTC-2.1 event times excluded). At SNR 8 and FAP 1e-3 ensemble TAP ~0.97 (BBH), ~0.55 (NSBH), ~0.08 (BNS) (read from Fig 3). Attribution: 1D model focuses on pre-merger data, 2D on the whole chirp.

models.title: Waves in a Forest: A Random Forest Classifier to Distinguish between Gravitational Waves and Detector Glitches
models.authors: Neev Shah, Alan M. Knee, Jess McIver, David Stenning
models.venue: arXiv preprint (no journal reference on arXiv record)
models.access: Open arXiv (PDF text read in full; confusion-matrix numbers taken from figure text, figures not viewed as images).
models.architecture: Two-stage: (1) Bayesian parameter estimation with Bilby/dynesty and the IMRPhenomXPHM precessing+HOM waveform on each 4 s single-detector sample (glitch or simulated GW) with common priors; (2) random forest (100 trees, Gini, unlimited depth, SMOTE-balanced training set) on ~200 posterior features (mode, median, 1- and 2-sigma widths, skew for each parameter plus pairwise linear correlations). Six-way classification: five glitch classes plus GW ("chirp"). Separate H1 and L1 classifiers.
models.inputs: Posterior-sample summary statistics (not raw strain) from single-detector PE of 4 s data.
models.data: 2,279 (H1) / 2,254 (L1) Gravity Spy glitches (>=95% confidence) from the Ashton et al. set across five classes (Table 1), real data; plus >300 simulated GWs per detector (masses 5-125 Msun grid, spin magnitudes 0-1, comoving-volume distance, O3 PSD synthetic noise, each re-drawn until SNR>=8).
models.training: Random forest, 70/30 train/test, SMOTE on training only, 100 repeats per detector; median confusion matrix and std reported. PE runs are the computational cost (not reported).
models.results: Mean accuracy 0.93 (H1) and 0.94 (L1); GW recall 0.90 (H1), 0.88 (L1), with ~10-12% of GWs labelled Blip. Fast scattering and scattered light are mutually confused (recalls 0.48-0.72). Modes alone give similar overall results (but Koi Fish recall drops 0.93 -> 0.64 at H1 and 0.97 -> 0.81 at L1). Most important features: modes/medians of chirp mass, total mass, median q, 2-sigma total-mass width.

models.gaps: Simulated GWs (Gaussian synthetic noise, SNR>=8) vs real-noise glitches (very high SNR): classes differ in noise provenance and SNR, so the classifier may exploit these; no real GW events tested; single-detector only; PE cost not given; no ROC/FAR curves; GW prior not astrophysical.

models.authors: Hongyu Shen, E. A. Huerta, Eamonn O'Shea, Prayush Kumar, Zhizhen Zhao
models.venue: Machine Learning: Science and Technology, Volume 3, Number 1, Year 2022

models.architecture: WaveNet encoder (11 dilated residual blocks, input 1 s at 4096 Hz, 254-dim feature vector) feeding a conditional autoregressive-spline normalizing flow (Pyro; 3 layers for masses, 8 layers for final spin and QNMs) that outputs a posterior; contrastive loss on the feature vectors (pairs of two noise realisations of the same template). models.title: Learning to detect continuous gravitational waves: an open data-analysis competition
models.authors: Rodrigo Tenorio, Michael J. Williams, Joseph Bayley, Christopher Messenger, Maggie Demkin, Walter Reade et al.
models.access: Open arXiv 2509.06445 (PDF text read in full via PDFKit extraction; Fig 5 viewed as image; other figures not viewed).
models.architecture: Not a single model: a Kaggle competition (G2Net CW, 4 Oct 2022 to 4 Jan 2023) whose top-10 solutions are described. Track-based statistics (JunKoda 1st: GPU maximum Dirichlet-weighted power over a square grid of 3.5e8 templates; PreferredWave 2nd: GPU average power, 3.3e6 uniformly sampled templates; HiddenNeuralLayers 5th and Shun_PI 6th: maximum power with differential-evolution / simulated-annealing template placement; SpaceCoders 4th: dynamic-programming track with one inflection point) and machine-learning solutions (BearWaves 3rd: ensemble of neural networks on time-averaged data, on-the-fly PyFstat training; KDL 7th; MC Digital 8th: CNN combined manually with F-statistic, separate Gaussian/real-data networks; yu4u 9th: U-net locating signal in spectrogram; anonamename 10th: CNN with detection statistic plus signal-location mask). Reference baseline: SOAP (Viterbi track, line-aware statistic).
models.inputs: Short Fourier Transforms (SFTs, T_SFT=1800 s) for H1 and L1, 4 months span, 0.2 Hz band (360 bins), with realistic science-mode/gap structure (duty cycle ~0.78); output is a per-sample ranking statistic.
models.data: 8,000 test samples (half signal, half noise) and 600 training samples released on Kaggle (~0.5 TB); simulated Gaussian noise (sqrt(Sn)=5e-24 Hz^-1/2) or real O3 LIGO noise (frequency labels shifted by up to 4 Hz, 0.1% Gaussian mangling). CW signals: f0 uniform 50-500 Hz, log-uniform spindown (90% negative 1e-12..1e-8 Hz/s, 10% positive), isotropic orientation, SNR drawn from Gamma(5, scale 9); 20% of signals above the re-scaled GCT sensitivity, ~41% above Weave, 6% visible (rho>80).

models.architecture: AttenGW framework: 12 neural architectures compared on O3a (TCN early-fusion, TCN separate stems + simple fusion, TCN+STFT, HDCN+cross-attention, HDCN+graph, BiMamba, ResNet, patch transformer, etc.); the selected early-fusion dilated TCN (kernel 7, 32 hidden channels, residual blocks with dilations up to 128, sigmoid per-timestep output) has 116k parameters; four independently seeded copies used.
